BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance 

BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance brings compliance activity from the Anthropic Claude Compliance API into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests Claude compliance events into Sentinel, giving security, risk, and audit teams centralized visibility into AI usage and related activity. By correlating these compliance signals with identity, endpoint, and other security telemetry, the integration supports threat hunting, investigation of policy violations and anomalous behavior, compliance monitoring, and repeatable audit workflows.  

Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel 

Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel brings security and network events from the Cato SASE Platform into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) Push pattern. The connector pushes events into a dedicated Log Analytics table, making Cato activity available alongside other Sentinel data. By centralizing this telemetry in Sentinel, the integration enables security teams to incorporate Cato events into threat hunting, detection, and visualization workflows alongside broader security signals.

Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector for Microsoft Sentinel 

The Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector brings threat intelligence from Check Point Exposure Management into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests indicators of compromise (IoCs), including malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with threat context such as confidence, severity, kill-chain stage, and campaign associations. An included playbook further enriches incident IoCs through ThreatCloud, helping security teams correlate intelligence with existing telemetry, accelerate triage and investigation, and reduce the manual effort required to maintain threat intelligence. 

Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel 

Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel brings threat intelligence from Check Point Infinity External Risk Management into Sentinel. The connector ingests malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with context such as severity, confidence, and detected activity. By correlating these indicators of compromise (IoCs) with existing logs through analytics rules, hunting queries, and watchlists, the integration helps security teams reduce manual intelligence management, identify matches with external threats, and accelerate threat detection and investigation. 

Citrix SPA Sentinel App

Citrix SPA Sentinel App brings Citrix Secure Private Access and Device Posture service events into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector imports critical logs, policy outcomes, and user activity data, giving security teams greater visibility into application access and device posture activity. An included workbook supports visualization and analysis of Citrix data, helping SOC teams correlate activity with broader security telemetry, investigate security risks, support compliance monitoring, and strengthen threat hunting across their environment.

ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel

ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings security delivery and administrative activity from ContraForce workspaces into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). ContraForce is an Agentic Security Delivery Platform for service providers and security teams running triage, investigation, and response across Microsoft Defender XDR and Sentinel. The connector ingests incidents, privileged access changes, service account credential activity, and high-impact workspace actions. Three included analytics rules detect privileged access, credential, and high-impact workspace activity, helping teams monitor and investigate the platform supporting their security operations.

Corelight for Microsoft Sentinel

By transforming all network traffic into rich, comprehensive evidence, Corelight gives security teams using Microsoft Sentinel the visibility to understand exactly what is happening across their enterprise networks. In addition to native integration with Microsoft Sentinel, Corelight integrates with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Defender Vulnerability Management, and Entra ID to streamline investigations, accelerate responses, and remediate incidents quickly and easily. The Corelight App for Microsoft Sentinel includes intuitive dashboards, pre-defined workbooks , sample queries, and analytics rules that help make SOC teams more efficient and effective.

CTM360

CTM360 brings external threat visibility into Microsoft Sentinel. The integration connects the CTM360 HackerView and CyberBlindspot platforms to Sentinel through REST APIs, so external attack surface and digital risk events flow straight into security operations workflows. HackerView surfaces externally exposed assets and security issues across your attack surface. CyberBlindspot adds organization-specific threat intelligence from surface, deep, and dark web monitoring. With these signals centralized in Sentinel, security teams can analyze external exposures alongside their broader telemetry and speed up detection, investigation, and response. 

Cyren CrowdStrike IOC Automation

Cyren CrowdStrike IOC Automation connects Cyren IP reputation threat intelligence with Microsoft Sentinel and CrowdStrike Falcon to operationalize malicious IP indicators. An included Logic App playbook automatically retrieves known malicious IP addresses from Cyren and submits them to CrowdStrike Falcon as custom indicators of compromise (IOCs) for blocking and detection. Scheduled execution keeps the intelligence updated and automates the flow of Cyren IP reputation data into CrowdStrike Falcon for blocking and detection.

Vaikora AI Agent Signals for Microsoft Sentinel

Vaikora AI Agent Signals for Microsoft Sentinel brings behavioral security signals from AI agents into Sentinel for centralized monitoring and response. The connector ingests risk scores, anomaly and threat classifications, policy enforcement decisions, and audit data, including signals for prompt injection attempts and suspicious tool usage. Included analytics rules and a workbook help security teams detect behavioral anomalies, investigate policy violations, and incorporate AI agent risks into existing Sentinel incident workflows.  

Vaikora AI Agent Signals for SentinelOne

Vaikora AI Agent Signals for SentinelOne brings high-risk behavioral security signals from Vaikora into SentinelOne as threat intelligence indicators of compromise (IOCs). The integration filters high-severity and anomalous AI agent activity and maps Vaikora risk scores to SentinelOne severity levels. The resulting IOCs are submitted to SentinelOne and expire after 90 days, enabling Vaikora security signals to be incorporated into SentinelOne endpoint protection workflows.

 

DataBahn Agentic Data Control Plane for Microsoft Sentinel

DataBahn’s agentic data control plane integrates with Microsoft Sentinel to provide our shared customers an AI-native data pipeline and orchestration platform that allows them to accelerate enterprise deployments. DataBahn’s pipeline standardizes onboarding and shaping across all data sources while providing operational visibility into data flow and health. Together, the collaboration focuses on reducing onboarding friction, improving normalization consistency, and enabling intentional routing, which helps security teams improve visibility, support threat detection, and streamline investigation and incident response workflows. 

Delinea Platform for Microsoft Sentinel

Delinea Platform Sentinel Solution brings privileged access activity into Sentinel natively through the Content Hub, as a complete SOC package. The connector pulls audit events covering secrets access, authentication, session activity and configuration changes directly into Sentinel. Ready-made workbooks, analytics rules with baseline-driven detection, hunting queries and an automated response playbook let security teams detect bulk secret access, failed sign-in bursts and privilege escalation sooner, investigate without leaving Sentinel and answer auditors with a record of what happened and why it was allowed.

Dynatrace Software Intelligence Platform with Microsoft Sentinel

Dynatrace integrates bidirectionally with Microsoft Sentinel, bringing application attacks, runtime vulnerabilities, Dynatrace Intelligence problems, and audit logs into Sentinel, where analytics rules, workbooks, and playbooks support detection, triage, and response. Sentinel can also send alerts to Dynatrace and enrich detected attacks with Sentinel and Microsoft Defender XDR insights. Bindplane by Dynatrace complements the integration by collecting and routing logs into Sentinel, including normalization to ASIM tables, giving SOC teams runtime and topology context for investigations.

ExtraHop RevealX for Microsoft Sentinel

ExtraHop RevealX for Microsoft Sentinel brings network detection and response (NDR) into Sentinel, giving your SOC visibility into threats that endpoint and log tools miss, including lateral movement and credential abuse hiding in encrypted east-west traffic. RevealX decrypts and analyzes network traffic at line rate, out of band with no impact on the network. The connector sends ExtraHop detections into Sentinel for dashboards, custom alerts, and investigation, so network context enriches your existing SOC workflows instead of sitting in a separate console.

Fire Compass  

FireCompass Risks for Microsoft Sentinel brings validated external risk findings from the FireCompass platform into Microsoft Sentinel through the Codeless Connector Framework. The connector ingests risk data including severity, affected assets, assessment context, impact, and remediation guidance. By making validated exposures available in Sentinel, security teams can correlate external risks with endpoint and network telemetry, track remediation progress, and build analytics rules, workbooks, and hunting queries on top of FireCompass findings. 

Gambit Security Sentinel Solution

Gambit brings resilience context into Microsoft Sentinel. It finds the resilience issues in your environment and syncs them to your Sentinel workspace daily, to help analysts see recovery risk before anything goes wrong. Sentinel correlates those issues with its detections. Your team can then prioritize the attacks most likely to disrupt critical operations: the ones hitting resources that aren’t ready to recover. Sentinel tells you what’s happening. Gambit tells you whether you can recover from it. 

Group-IB Threat Intelligence Integration with Azure 

Group-IB Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel brings adversary-centric threat intelligence into Sentinel, including malicious IPs, domains, URLs, and file hashes with risk scores and malware attribution. Additional intelligence on threat actors, malware, vulnerabilities, data leaks, compromised credentials, and suspicious payment details are available for hunting and visualization. Enrichment playbooks also let analysts add Group-IB context, WHOIS data, and IP scoring directly to incidents, supporting threat investigation and analysis.   

Holm Security for Microsoft Sentinel 

Holm Security for Microsoft Sentinel brings asset data from the Holm Security platform into Sentinel via the Holm Security REST API. The connector ingests web and network assets into Microsoft Sentinel, including metadata such as IP addresses, hostnames, operating systems, tags, and vulnerability counts per asset. By incorporating this asset inventory alongside other security telemetry, the integration enables security teams to build dashboards, create custom alerts, and correlate asset information with other data in Microsoft Sentinel. 

 

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager for Microsoft Sentinel 

The Idira® Endpoint Privilege Manager by Palo Alto Networks integration for Microsoft Sentinel pulls application events and policy audit activity into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework and the Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager REST API. Events land in a dedicated Log Analytics table, so security teams can analyze privilege activity alongside their other telemetry and build detections. 

 

IPinfo: IP geolocation & intelligence database

IPinfo: IP geolocation & intelligence database brings contextual IP intelligence into Microsoft Sentinel to enrich security logs and investigations. The solution provides data such as IP geolocation, network ownership and routing, proxy and residential proxy detection, ASN information, and other IP classifications. By adding this context to IP addresses observed in Sentinel, the integration helps security teams better understand indicators of compromise, prioritize security events, strengthen threat detection and investigation, and inform network and access management decisions. 

 

Island Solution for Microsoft Sentinel

Island Solution for Microsoft Sentinel brings user activity and administrative audit events from the Island Enterprise Browser into Microsoft Sentinel for centralized security monitoring. The solution automatically shares events from the Island Management Console with Sentinel and includes data connectors and workbooks for user activity and admin audit logs. By adding browser activity context to existing security telemetry, the integration helps security teams monitor and analyze user and administrative activity and investigate potential security issues.

 

NetApp Ransomware Resilience for Microsoft Sentinel

NetApp Ransomware Resilience detects and contains ransomware attacks on NetApp ONTAP workloads in real time, then enables fast, clean recovery. Its Microsoft Sentinel integration enriches alerts with data-layer context, including attack type, severity, user and IP, and affected cluster, volume, and SVM. The NetApp SOAR playbook can take actions on ONTAP such as trigger immutable snapshots, block suspicious users or IPs, and take compromised volumes offline. Together, these integrations extend the NetApp Platform’s ability to help security teams triage and respond to ransomware attacks, limit data loss, protect recovery points, and coordinate response across storage and security teams. 

 

NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel

NordLayer Intelligence by NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel brings external threat and exposure findings into Sentinel through the Azure Monitor Logs Ingestion API. The integration provides findings including leaked credentials, breach exposures, malware and info-stealer infections, dark web activity, domain impersonation risks, and external attack surface vulnerabilities. By correlating these findings with other security telemetry in Sentinel, the solution helps teams investigate external threats, identify exposures affecting their organization, and automate triage and response through analytics rules and SOAR playbooks.

 

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel brings third-party security findings from the Panorays platform into Sentinel through the Panorays API. The connector provides security teams with visibility into the security posture of vendors and supply-chain organizations, making third-party risk and vulnerability findings available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating Panorays findings into Sentinel workflows, the integration helps SOC teams centrally monitor and investigate third-party risks and correlate them with internal security signals.

 

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector brings compromised credential intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests alerts for exposed corporate credentials, enabling security teams to investigate potential account takeover risks within existing Sentinel workflows. Included analytics can identify newly compromised credentials and successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-ins involving known-compromised accounts, helping SOC teams operationalize external credential intelligence and prioritize investigation and response.

 

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel brings curated indicators of compromise (IoCs) from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Stream into Microsoft Sentinel Threat Intelligence. The integration provides indicators including malicious URLs, phishing sites, and malware hashes derived from PRODAFT investigations. By making these indicators available for correlation with existing telemetry, hunting queries, and detection rules, the solution helps security teams identify connections to malicious infrastructure, investigate phishing and malware activity, and incorporate external threat intelligence into existing triage and response workflows.

 

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector brings compromised payment card intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector retrieves alerts associated with an organization’s payment card BIN ranges and makes them available within Sentinel for investigation. Included analytics identify newly exposed and non-expired compromised cards, helping security teams centralize payment fraud intelligence, prioritize potentially actionable exposures, and incorporate them into existing investigation and response workflows.

 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel brings audit logs from Pulumi, the infrastructure platform for humans and agents, into Microsoft Sentinel through the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests authentication events, organization membership changes, stack lifecycle operations, policy changes, and access token usage. It also includes three analytics rules that detect failed login attempts, stack deletions, and organization membership changes. Your security team can see what a human or agent did, when, and where across infrastructure as code, secrets, configuration, and policies, which helps speed up security and governance investigations.  

 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel brings post-quantum cryptography readiness findings from Azure environments into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector provides visibility into cryptographic assets including Key Vault keys, TLS certificates and configurations, and Entra ID app registration certificates, with quantum posture ratings and risk scores. Included are six analytics rules, a workbook, and a notification playbook to help security teams identify vulnerable cryptographic assets and prioritize post-quantum migration planning. 

 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel brings identity security telemetry from SailPoint Identity Security Cloud into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The solution streams audit and search events into Sentinel tables, where analysts can correlate identity activity with other security signals and query SailPoint APIs for additional identity and account context during incident triage. Automated playbooks can also remediate threats by revoking access or disabling compromised accounts, helping teams connect identity insight with investigation and response.

 

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition extends Microsoft Sentinel security monitoring for SAP RISE environments with infrastructure, database, operating system, and network security logs managed by SAP Enterprise Cloud Services. Deployed alongside the Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP applications, it complements application-layer monitoring to provide visibility across the SAP stack and enable cross-layer threat detection and correlation. The solution supports near real-time log collection, built-in analytics and workbooks, ASIM-based security content, and correlation with signals from endpoints, Microsoft Entra ID, and other sources in Microsoft Sentinel.   

 

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel brings suspicious email data analyzed by users through Secure Practice MailRisk into Sentinel. The connector ingests enriched email metadata and risk assessment updates from the Secure Practice API, providing potential indicators of compromise identified from reported emails. By incorporating MailRisk data alongside other security telemetry, the integration helps security teams correlate suspicious email activity, search and investigate potential threats, and incorporate user-reported email intelligence into alerting and incident response workflows. 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel provides cybersecurity posture ratings based on continuously monitored risk factors and threat intelligence. SecurityScorecard evaluates organizations using an A-F rating, helping security teams identify and track cybersecurity risks. The solution supports use cases including enterprise cyber risk management, third-party risk monitoring, executive reporting, and cyber due diligence. 

 

SIGNL4 - Mobile Alerting & Response for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud

SIGNL4 bridges the gap between security detection and human response with mobile-first alerting and incident management for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud. Its two-way integrations allow security teams to acknowledge, escalate, and resolve incidents directly from their mobile devices, with updates automatically synchronized back to Sentinel. Critical Defender for Cloud findings trigger actionable response workflows, while persistent mobile notifications, automated escalations, and on-call scheduling ensure the right people are reached when it matters most. The result is faster incident response, clear accountability, and a fully auditable process - wherever responders are.


SOC Prime Audit CCP

SOC Prime Audit CCP brings SOC Prime Platform audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel for centralized security monitoring and analysis. The connector ingests platform activity including user actions, API calls, and administrative events, providing an audit trail across detection engineering processes. By correlating SOC Prime activity with other security signals in Sentinel, the integration helps security teams investigate platform activity, support compliance monitoring, and incorporate audit telemetry into broader threat detection and response workflows. 

 

SOCRadar Alerts Azure Sentinel Directional Solution

SOCRadar Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel enriches security operations by bringing prioritized, context-rich alerts directly into Microsoft Sentinel. Covering SOCRadar’s Extended Threat Intelligence capabilities, including Brand Protection, External Attack Surface Management (ASM), Third-Party Findings, and other security modules, the integration helps organizations monitor external threats and manage investigations within their existing SOC workflows. Bidirectional synchronization also helps keep incident status, severity, and comments aligned between Microsoft Sentinel and SOCRadar.

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel  

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel brings stolen identity data from infostealer malware, phishing attacks, and third-party breaches into Microsoft Sentinel, helping security teams uncover compromised identities, prioritize high-risk exposures, and accelerate remediation to prevent session hijacking and other targeted identity-based attacks. The solution includes a custom API connector, a Logic Apps playbook for ingesting data into Log Analytics, analytic rules that generate Sentinel incidents from breach and malware data, and additional Logic Apps playbooks for incident automation and enrichment. 

 

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel brings asset and vulnerability data from Tenable One Vulnerability Management into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The integration combines Tenable cyber exposure insights with Sentinel’s collection, detection, and investigation capabilities, making vulnerability context available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating asset and vulnerability findings into Sentinel workflows, the solution helps security teams correlate exposure data with security signals, investigate risks affecting vulnerable assets, and better prioritize remediation efforts.

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings authentication, credential access and management, sharing, administrative activity, and platform threat detections into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Included analytics rules identify scenarios such as sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses, excessive credential access, data exports, and security policy or privilege changes. A workbook visualizes activity and threat detections, helping security teams monitor password-management activity, investigate potential credential risks, and correlate findings with broader security telemetry. 

 

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager (ESKM) integrates with Microsoft Sentinel to provide centralized security monitoring and visibility into cryptographic key management activities through KMIP server logs. The solution enables organizations to monitor key operations, KMIP client activity, and authentication events, helping security teams identify suspicious behavior and investigate potential threats. Built-in analytics rules help detect brute-force authentication attempts, repeated permission-denied events, and key-destruction activity, while hunting queries and a dedicated workbook support deeper investigation of unusual users, source IPs, key retrieval patterns, and after-hours activity. 

 

valimail-sentinel-enforce

Valimail enables organizations to see who sends email using your domain, protects against domain impersonation, and displays a verified logo in inboxes to increase brand trust. Our Microsoft Sentinel Connector brings Valimail Enforce event data directly into Sentinel, allowing security teams to incorporate our telemetry into unified SIEM workflows, monitor authentication and enforcement trends in real time, and build custom alerts and visualizations based on DMARC events. Once configured, Sentinel continuously ingests Valimail event logs, enriching your broader security intelligence and helping to improve your ability to detect and respond to threats across your environment. 

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions brings enriched, data-centric Varonis alerts into Microsoft Sentinel for triage, investigation, and remediation. Varonis insights are contextualized alongside other security events to provide a unified view of data risk. This allows security teams to view and close Varonis alerts directly within Sentinel, reducing the need to switch interfaces and supporting incident resolution with less manual effort

Whisper for Sentinel

Whisper for Sentinel enriches Microsoft Sentinel incidents and alerts with threat and infrastructure intelligence for IPs, domains, ASNs, and networks. The solution provides threat scores, supporting evidence, infrastructure relationships, and historical context directly within Sentinel. Included enrichment playbooks, analytics rules, hunting queries, and workbooks support investigation of threats including C2 communications, malicious infrastructure, suspicious domains, and BGP anomalies, while retained enrichment data can be queried and correlated with existing logs.

WhoisFreaks Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel  

The WhoisFreaks solution for Microsoft Sentinel brings domain threat intelligence and newly registered domain (NRD) data into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Customers can connect malware, phishing, and spam threat feeds, along with gTLD and ccTLD NRD feeds with or without WHOIS data. Included analytics rule templates help identify high-confidence malicious domains, newly registered domains appearing in threat feeds, threat-listed parked domains, and unusual NRD volumes that may indicate bulk registration activity. 

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel  

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel brings Wiz Issues, Vulnerability Findings, and Audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel. Wiz identifies and prioritizes cloud security risks across areas including vulnerabilities, malware, internet exposure, identity, and data security in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, Alibaba, and Kubernetes environments. 

 

In addition to the solutions from our third-party partners, we are also excited to announce the following connectors published by the Microsoft Sentinel team:

Building a more connected foundation for security operations 

The strength of the connector ecosystem reflects the work of Microsoft and our technology partners to support our shared customers. Together, we are helping organizations connect the technologies they rely on and bring more of their security data into a unified operational experience. 

For customers 

If you are a Microsoft Sentinel or ISOC customer, or considering adopting it, we want you to have the security connectors and integrations you need to get value from the platform. If an integration with an independent software vendor (ISV) is not yet available, or you have an issue with an existing solution, we have a dedicated team that may be able to assist by working with ISVs to build new or update existing connectors. 

For software companies 

If you are a software development partner, the Microsoft Sentinel Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) provides a streamlined way to bring your product into the Microsoft Security ecosystem. Partners can also work directly with Microsoft for engineering guidance and support to build or improve a connector. 

Building a more connected foundation for security operations 

Our goal is simple: help customers protect their digital environments by giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete picture of risk. We’ll continue investing in connectors, partnerships, and integrated security experiences to help customers defend their organizations with greater visibility, context, and confidence.

items.title: Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization
items.summary: AWS Sign-In is introducing support for Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), enabling organizations to securely authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through their existing enterprise identity providers (IdPs), such as Okta. With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users to manage additional long-term credentials or complete separate consent flows. In our previous blog post, Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server , we introduced OAuth-based authorization, enabling AI agents to securely access AWS MCP Server through interactive sign-in or programmatic authentication using AWS credentials. EMA builds on these capabilities by enabling organizations to authorize AI agents through their existing enterprise IdPs. Because authentication to an AI application doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources, EMA provides a way to authorize access across these separate trust domains while maintaining existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. In this post, we explain how EMA and ID-JAG work with AWS Sign-In , discuss security best practices, and walk you through configuring Okta to authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server. How Enterprise-Managed Authorization works with AWS Sign-In Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enables organizations to centrally manage how AI applications access protected resources on behalf of employees. EMA uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), an OAuth-based authorization grant that enables enterprise IdPs to authorize access across different trust domains. Rather than requiring employees to individually authorize each MCP server, administrators can define policies in their existing IdP to control which AI applications can access specific resources. When an employee signs in to an AI application such as Claude using their enterprise IdP, the authentication establishes their identity within Claude but doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources. When the AI application requests access to an MCP server, the enterprise IdP evaluates its configured access policies and issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion for the intended resource. The AI application then exchanges this assertion with the authorization server configured for the MCP server to obtain an OAuth access token, without requiring the employee to complete an additional interactive authorization flow. For AWS MCP Server, AWS Sign-In serves as the configured OAuth authorization server. The AI application presents the ID-JAG assertion to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. As part of the authorization process, AWS validates the assertion against the trusted IdP and uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to evaluate the IAM role’s trust policy and establish the authorized role session. AWS Sign-In then issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. IAM policies attached to the role determine which AWS operations the agent can perform, allowing organizations to manage agent authorization through their enterprise IdP while enforcing existing AWS permissions. Figure 1 illustrates how an AI application, such as Claude, uses EMA with Okta and AWS Sign-In to obtain an OAuth access token and securely access AWS MCP Server using IAM role-based permissions. Figure 1: Enterprise-Managed Authorization flow using Okta, AWS Sign-In, and AWS MCP Server The authorization flow consists of the following steps, as illustrated in Figure 1: Employee authentication: The employee signs in to the AI application, such as Claude, using their enterprise IdP, such as Okta, through single sign-on (SSO). ID-JAG request: When the AI application needs to access AWS MCP Server, it requests an ID-JAG from Okta for the intended resource. Enterprise authorization: Okta evaluates the configured access policies to determine whether the employee and AI application are authorized to access AWS MCP Server. If authorized, Okta issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion. Token exchange with AWS Sign-In: The AI application sends the ID-JAG to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion, including its issuer, signature, audience/tenant, expiration, and intended resource, and verifies the associated IAM role authorization before issuing an OAuth access token. Access AWS MCP Server: The AI application presents the AWS-issued OAuth access token to AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and access to AWS resources is governed by the permissions associated with the IAM role. Configure Enterprise-Managed Authorization using Okta and AWS Sign-In In this section, we walk you through configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) to enable an AI application, such as Claude, to securely access AWS MCP Server using an enterprise identity managed in Okta. The configuration establishes trust between Okta and AWS, defines IAM permissions for accessing AWS resources, and configures enterprise authorization policies that govern AI application access. This walkthrough uses AWS MCP Server in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region ( us-west-2 ). Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have the following: An AWS account with permissions to configure IAM IdPs, roles, and policies. An Okta organization with administrative permissions to manage applications and configure Cross-App Access policies. An AI application, such as Claude, that supports EMA and ID-JAG. Access to AWS MCP Server with support for OAuth-based Enterprise-Managed Authorization. The AWS Region where you will configure the integration. Step 0: Configure the AI application in Okta Configure an application in Okta so that employees can sign in to the AI application through enterprise single sign-on (SSO). For this walkthrough, we use Claude as the AI application. If your organization already uses Claude with Okta SSO, you can use the existing application. This application is the requesting application when you configure Cross-App Access in Step 3. Create the Claude SSO application : In the Okta Admin Console, go to Applications , choose Create App Integration , and create an OIDC web application, for example Claude SSO, as shown in Figure 2. If your agent was imported through an Okta AI Agent Provider , create the OIDC application by going to Directory , AI Agents , then navigating to User access from the selected agent. Choose the grant types : Select Authorization Code and Refresh Token . Claude uses the refresh token to request new ID-JAG assertions without asking employees to sign in again. Add the redirect URI: Set Sign-in redirect URIs to Claude’s SSO callback URL. Assign employees: Under Assignments , select which employees or groups can access the application. Confirm SSO works: Check that employees can sign in to Claude through Okta before you continue. Figure 2: Creating the Claude SSO app integration in Okta Step 1: Configure Okta as an OIDC IdP in IAM Create an OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP so that AWS trusts the ID-JAG assertions that Okta issues, as shown in Figure 3. Add the IdP: In the AWS Management Console for IAM, go to Identity providers , choose Add provider, and select OpenID Connect . Enter the provider URL: For Provider URL , enter your Okta org URL, for example https://integrator-1234567.okta.com . Okta issues ID-JAG assertions from the org authorization server, not from a custom authorization server. Enter the audience: For Audience , enter the AWS Sign-In authorization server for your Region, for example https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws , and choose Add provider . Figure 3: Adding Okta as an OpenID Connect identity provider in IAM Step 2: Create an IAM role and configure permissions Create an IAM role that defines the AWS permissions granted to the AI application, as shown in Figure 4. Create the role: In the IAM console, go to Roles , choose Create role , and select Web identity as the trusted entity type. Choose the Okta IdP from Step 1 and its audience. This creates a trust policy that allows access only through assertions from that provider. Attach the AWS MCP Server permissions: Attach the AWS managed policy AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy . It grants the signin:CreateOAuth2Token permission required for OAuth access to AWS MCP Server. Attach the AWS permissions the AI application needs: Attach other IAM policies that grant only the AWS permissions required by the AI application. For this walkthrough, we use a read-only role. Name and create the role: Enter a role name, for example OktaAwsMcpReadOnly , and choose Create role . Copy the role ARN: You’ll enter the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the Audience/tenant ID in Okta in Step 3. Figure 4: Reviewing the IAM role and its trust policy Step 3: Configure Cross-App Access in Okta In the Okta Admin Console, create a resource application that represents AWS MCP Server, and then connect Claude to it. The Claude SSO App from Step 0 stays the requesting application, so you don’t enable Cross-App Access on it. Create the AWS MCP resource application: Go to Applications , choose Create App Integration , and create an OIDC web application, for example AWS MCP (us-west-2). Okta doesn’t use this application’s sign-in redirect URI, so you can keep the default value. Figure 5: Creating the AWS MCP resource application in Okta Enable Cross-App Access on the resource application: On the Machine Assignments tab, edit the access method and enable Cross-App Access. Set Issuer URL to https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws and set Audience/tenant ID to the IAM role ARN from Step 2. Figure 6: Enabling Cross-App Access on the AWS MCP resource application Assign employees: On the Assignments tab, assign the employees or groups who can access AWS MCP Server through Claude. Register Claude as an AI agent: Go to Directory , AI Agents, and choose Register AI agent . Under User access , choose Select an existing app and pick the Claude SSO App from Step 0. Skip this step if the agent was already imported via an Okta AI Agent Provider . Connect the AI agent to AWS MCP Server: On the AI agent page, add a resource connection with the Application resource type. Set Application instance to the AWS MCP resource application. Set the client ID registered in AWS MCP to the client ID that you configure in Claude in Step 4, for example anthropic-claude . Set Resource identifier to https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp . Figure 7: Connecting the Claude AI agent to the AWS MCP resource application When Claude requests access, Okta checks that the employee is assigned access and issues an ID-JAG for AWS Sign-In that carries the IAM role ARN. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion and issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. Step 4: Configure Claude to access AWS MCP Server Add a custom connector: In Claude, open Admin settings , choose Connectors , and then choose Add, Custom connector . Enter a name and the AWS MCP Server endpoint, for example https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp . Configure OAuth authentication: For Authentication , choose Sign in when needed . For OAuth client , choose Use your own OAuth client , enter the client ID from the resource connection in Step 3 and leave the client secret blank. Figure 8: Adding AWS MCP Server as a custom connector in Claude Set up managed authorization: Open the connector, and on the Configuration tab, choose Set up next to Managed authorization . Figure 9: The connector’s Configuration tab Configure IdP-managed access: Choose IdP-managed as the identity source and confirm that the connection checks pass. Then choose Continue , select the Claude roles that connect through managed authorization, and choose Save. Figure 10: Setting up managed authorization with Okta as the identity source When an employee accesses AWS MCP Server, Claude requests an ID-JAG assertion from Okta. Following successful policy evaluation, Okta issues the assertion, which Claude exchanges at the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint for an OAuth access token associated with the configured IAM role. Claude uses this token to access AWS MCP Server without requiring an additional AWS sign-in. Step 5: Validate access to AWS MCP Server To validate the configuration: Sign in using enterprise SSO: Sign in to the AI application using your Okta identity. Figure 11: Signing in to Claude with SSO Connect to AWS MCP Server : Connect the AI application to AWS MCP Server. Verify OAuth token issuance: Confirm that Claude successfully connects to AWS MCP Server without requiring a separate AWS authorization flow. You can verify successful OAuth token issuance using AWS CloudTrail, as described in Step 6. Validate authorized access: Perform an AWS operation permitted by the configured IAM role. Figure 12: Calling AWS MCP Server from Claude Code Verify access restrictions: Attempt an operation outside the IAM role’s permissions and confirm that access is denied. You can also validate enterprise authorization policies by attempting access using an employee who is not authorized in Okta and verifying that the ID-JAG request is denied. Step 6: Verify authorization activity using AWS CloudTrail AWS Sign-In and AWS MCP Server integrate with AWS CloudTrail to help organizations monitor OAuth authorization activity and API requests made by AI applications. CloudTrail provides visibility into token issuance, the applications requesting access, and operations performed through AWS MCP Server. After successfully connecting your AI application to AWS MCP Server, you can verify the authorization activity in CloudTrail: Open the CloudTrail console and navigate to Event history . Select the AWS Region used for the integration. Filter events by Event source signin.amazonaws.com or Event name CreateOAuth2Token to locate OAuth token issuance activity. Review the event details, including the OAuth client identifier, target resource, authorization grant type, and token issuance status, where recorded. To review subsequent MCP activity, examine events from aws-mcp.amazonaws .com with the same session ARN and verify that the operations performed by the AI application match the permissions configured for the IAM role. For more information, see Monitoring OAuth activity and Logging AWS MCP Server API calls using AWS CloudTrail . Best practices for securing AI agent access with EMA and AWS IAM When configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA), consider the following security recommendations to help protect AI agent access to AWS resources: Use short-lived ID-JAG assertions: Configure your enterprise IdP to issue ID-JAG assertions with short expiration periods. This limits the time during which an assertion can be exchanged for an OAuth access token and reduces the risk associated with token exposure. Use tenant-specific IdP issuers: In multi-tenant environments, configure tenant-specific issuer URLs to establish explicit trust relationships between AWS and the intended enterprise IdP. This helps prevent assertions issued for one tenant from being accepted in another tenant’s authorization context. Restrict OAuth authorization using IAM condition keys: Use IAM condition keys to limit OAuth token issuance to approved AI applications, authorization flows, and AWS resources. For example, use signin:OAuthClientId to restrict access to approved AI applications, such as arn:aws:signin:::external-client/jwt-bearer/anthropic-claude and signin:OAuthGrantType to restrict the permitted grant type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer . Apply least-privilege IAM permissions: Grant the IAM role only the permissions required by the AI application. Use managed policies to control which AWS operations the agent can perform through AWS MCP Server, reducing the impact of unauthorized or unintended actions. For more information about available IAM condition keys and permissions, see the AWS Sign-In condition keys reference and the AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy documentation. Conclusion Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) with AWS Sign-In enables organizations to securely connect AI agents to AWS resources using their existing enterprise IdPs. By combining centralized authorization policies with IAM permissions, organizations can control which AI applications access their resources while reducing the need for employees to manage AWS credentials or complete additional authorization flows. Using ID-JAG, AWS Sign-In exchanges enterprise-issued identity assertions for short-lived OAuth access tokens associated with IAM roles. This approach helps organizations enforce least-privilege access, reduce credential exposure, and simplify how employees securely access AWS resources through AI agents. To get started, see the Sign-in with OAuth 2.0 , Configure EMA for MCP servers , and Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server to learn more about OAuth-based access to AWS resources. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Outside of technology, Vaibhav enjoys traveling and exploring new cultures and cuisines. Jaimin Bhatt Jaimin is a Principal Software Engineer at AWS. Seling Chen Seling is a Senior Software Engineer on the AWS Identity Sign-In team, which focuses on securing access to the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, and MCP servers. Her contributions include OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, data perimeter enforcement in AWS Sign-In, and multi-session support for the console.
items.summary_html:
AWS Sign-In is introducing support for Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), enabling organizations to securely authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through their existing enterprise identity providers (IdPs), such as Okta. With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users to manage additional long-term credentials or complete separate consent flows.

In our previous blog post, Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server, we introduced OAuth-based authorization, enabling AI agents to securely access AWS MCP Server through interactive sign-in or programmatic authentication using AWS credentials. EMA builds on these capabilities by enabling organizations to authorize AI agents through their existing enterprise IdPs. Because authentication to an AI application doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources, EMA provides a way to authorize access across these separate trust domains while maintaining existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.

In this post, we explain how EMA and ID-JAG work with AWS Sign-In, discuss security best practices, and walk you through configuring Okta to authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server.

How Enterprise-Managed Authorization works with AWS Sign-In

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enables organizations to centrally manage how AI applications access protected resources on behalf of employees. EMA uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), an OAuth-based authorization grant that enables enterprise IdPs to authorize access across different trust domains. Rather than requiring employees to individually authorize each MCP server, administrators can define policies in their existing IdP to control which AI applications can access specific resources.

When an employee signs in to an AI application such as Claude using their enterprise IdP, the authentication establishes their identity within Claude but doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources. When the AI application requests access to an MCP server, the enterprise IdP evaluates its configured access policies and issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion for the intended resource. The AI application then exchanges this assertion with the authorization server configured for the MCP server to obtain an OAuth access token, without requiring the employee to complete an additional interactive authorization flow.

For AWS MCP Server, AWS Sign-In serves as the configured OAuth authorization server. The AI application presents the ID-JAG assertion to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. As part of the authorization process, AWS validates the assertion against the trusted IdP and uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to evaluate the IAM role’s trust policy and establish the authorized role session. AWS Sign-In then issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. IAM policies attached to the role determine which AWS operations the agent can perform, allowing organizations to manage agent authorization through their enterprise IdP while enforcing existing AWS permissions.

Figure 1 illustrates how an AI application, such as Claude, uses EMA with Okta and AWS Sign-In to obtain an OAuth access token and securely access AWS MCP Server using IAM role-based permissions.

Figure 1: Enterprise-Managed Authorization flow using Okta, AWS Sign-In, and AWS MCP Server

The authorization flow consists of the following steps, as illustrated in Figure 1:

  1. Employee authentication: The employee signs in to the AI application, such as Claude, using their enterprise IdP, such as Okta, through single sign-on (SSO).
  2. ID-JAG request: When the AI application needs to access AWS MCP Server, it requests an ID-JAG from Okta for the intended resource.
  3. Enterprise authorization: Okta evaluates the configured access policies to determine whether the employee and AI application are authorized to access AWS MCP Server. If authorized, Okta issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion.
  4. Token exchange with AWS Sign-In: The AI application sends the ID-JAG to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion, including its issuer, signature, audience/tenant, expiration, and intended resource, and verifies the associated IAM role authorization before issuing an OAuth access token.
  5. Access AWS MCP Server: The AI application presents the AWS-issued OAuth access token to AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and access to AWS resources is governed by the permissions associated with the IAM role.
Configure Enterprise-Managed Authorization using Okta and AWS Sign-In

In this section, we walk you through configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) to enable an AI application, such as Claude, to securely access AWS MCP Server using an enterprise identity managed in Okta.

The configuration establishes trust between Okta and AWS, defines IAM permissions for accessing AWS resources, and configures enterprise authorization policies that govern AI application access. This walkthrough uses AWS MCP Server in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region (us-west-2).

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to configure IAM IdPs, roles, and policies.
  • An Okta organization with administrative permissions to manage applications and configure Cross-App Access policies.
  • An AI application, such as Claude, that supports EMA and ID-JAG.
  • Access to AWS MCP Server with support for OAuth-based Enterprise-Managed Authorization.
  • The AWS Region where you will configure the integration.
Step 0: Configure the AI application in Okta

Configure an application in Okta so that employees can sign in to the AI application through enterprise single sign-on (SSO). For this walkthrough, we use Claude as the AI application. If your organization already uses Claude with Okta SSO, you can use the existing application. This application is the requesting application when you configure Cross-App Access in Step 3.

  1. Create the Claude SSO application: In the Okta Admin Console, go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example Claude SSO, as shown in Figure 2.
    • If your agent was imported through an Okta AI Agent Provider, create the OIDC application by going to Directory, AI Agents, then navigating to User access from the selected agent.
  2. Choose the grant types: Select Authorization Code and Refresh Token. Claude uses the refresh token to request new ID-JAG assertions without asking employees to sign in again.
  3. Add the redirect URI: Set Sign-in redirect URIs to Claude’s SSO callback URL.
  4. Assign employees: Under Assignments, select which employees or groups can access the application.
  5. Confirm SSO works: Check that employees can sign in to Claude through Okta before you continue.

Figure 2: Creating the Claude SSO app integration in Okta

Step 1: Configure Okta as an OIDC IdP in IAM

Create an OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP so that AWS trusts the ID-JAG assertions that Okta issues, as shown in Figure 3.

  1. Add the IdP: In the AWS Management Console for IAM, go to Identity providers, choose Add provider, and select OpenID Connect.
  2. Enter the provider URL: For Provider URL, enter your Okta org URL, for example https://integrator-1234567.okta.com. Okta issues ID-JAG assertions from the org authorization server, not from a custom authorization server.
  3. Enter the audience: For Audience, enter the AWS Sign-In authorization server for your Region, for example https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws, and choose Add provider.

Figure 3: Adding Okta as an OpenID Connect identity provider in IAM

Step 2: Create an IAM role and configure permissions

Create an IAM role that defines the AWS permissions granted to the AI application, as shown in Figure 4.

  1. Create the role: In the IAM console, go to Roles, choose Create role, and select Web identity as the trusted entity type. Choose the Okta IdP from Step 1 and its audience. This creates a trust policy that allows access only through assertions from that provider.
  2. Attach the AWS MCP Server permissions: Attach the AWS managed policy AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy. It grants the signin:CreateOAuth2Token permission required for OAuth access to AWS MCP Server.
  3. Attach the AWS permissions the AI application needs: Attach other IAM policies that grant only the AWS permissions required by the AI application. For this walkthrough, we use a read-only role.
  4. Name and create the role: Enter a role name, for example OktaAwsMcpReadOnly, and choose Create role.
  5. Copy the role ARN: You’ll enter the role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the Audience/tenant ID in Okta in Step 3.

Figure 4: Reviewing the IAM role and its trust policy

Step 3: Configure Cross-App Access in Okta

In the Okta Admin Console, create a resource application that represents AWS MCP Server, and then connect Claude to it. The Claude SSO App from Step 0 stays the requesting application, so you don’t enable Cross-App Access on it.

  1. Create the AWS MCP resource application: Go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example AWS MCP (us-west-2). Okta doesn’t use this application’s sign-in redirect URI, so you can keep the default value.

    Figure 5: Creating the AWS MCP resource application in Okta

  2. Enable Cross-App Access on the resource application: On the Machine Assignments tab, edit the access method and enable Cross-App Access. Set Issuer URL to https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws and set Audience/tenant ID to the IAM role ARN from Step 2.

    Figure 6: Enabling Cross-App Access on the AWS MCP resource application

  3. Assign employees: On the Assignments tab, assign the employees or groups who can access AWS MCP Server through Claude.
  4. Register Claude as an AI agent: Go to Directory, AI Agents, and choose Register AI agent. Under User access, choose Select an existing app and pick the Claude SSO App from Step 0.
    • Skip this step if the agent was already imported via an Okta AI Agent Provider.
  5. Connect the AI agent to AWS MCP Server: On the AI agent page, add a resource connection with the Application resource type. Set Application instance to the AWS MCP resource application. Set the client ID registered in AWS MCP to the client ID that you configure in Claude in Step 4, for example anthropic-claude. Set Resource identifier to https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.

    Figure 7: Connecting the Claude AI agent to the AWS MCP resource application

When Claude requests access, Okta checks that the employee is assigned access and issues an ID-JAG for AWS Sign-In that carries the IAM role ARN. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion and issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role.

Step 4: Configure Claude to access AWS MCP Server
  1. Add a custom connector: In Claude, open Admin settings, choose Connectors, and then choose Add, Custom connector. Enter a name and the AWS MCP Server endpoint, for example https://aws-mcp.us-west-2.api.aws/mcp.
  2. Configure OAuth authentication: For Authentication, choose Sign in when needed. For OAuth client, choose Use your own OAuth client, enter the client ID from the resource connection in Step 3 and leave the client secret blank.

    Figure 8: Adding AWS MCP Server as a custom connector in Claude

  3. Set up managed authorization: Open the connector, and on the Configuration tab, choose Set up next to Managed authorization.

    Figure 9: The connector’s Configuration tab

  4. Configure IdP-managed access: Choose IdP-managed as the identity source and confirm that the connection checks pass. Then choose Continue, select the Claude roles that connect through managed authorization, and choose Save.

    Figure 10: Setting up managed authorization with Okta as the identity source

When an employee accesses AWS MCP Server, Claude requests an ID-JAG assertion from Okta. Following successful policy evaluation, Okta issues the assertion, which Claude exchanges at the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint for an OAuth access token associated with the configured IAM role. Claude uses this token to access AWS MCP Server without requiring an additional AWS sign-in.

Step 5: Validate access to AWS MCP Server

To validate the configuration:

  1. Sign in using enterprise SSO: Sign in to the AI application using your Okta identity.

    Figure 11: Signing in to Claude with SSO

  2. Connect to AWS MCP Server: Connect the AI application to AWS MCP Server.
  3. Verify OAuth token issuance: Confirm that Claude successfully connects to AWS MCP Server without requiring a separate AWS authorization flow. You can verify successful OAuth token issuance using AWS CloudTrail, as described in Step 6.
  4. Validate authorized access: Perform an AWS operation permitted by the configured IAM role.

    Figure 12: Calling AWS MCP Server from Claude Code

  5. Verify access restrictions: Attempt an operation outside the IAM role’s permissions and confirm that access is denied.

You can also validate enterprise authorization policies by attempting access using an employee who is not authorized in Okta and verifying that the ID-JAG request is denied.

Step 6: Verify authorization activity using AWS CloudTrail

AWS Sign-In and AWS MCP Server integrate with AWS CloudTrail to help organizations monitor OAuth authorization activity and API requests made by AI applications. CloudTrail provides visibility into token issuance, the applications requesting access, and operations performed through AWS MCP Server.

After successfully connecting your AI application to AWS MCP Server, you can verify the authorization activity in CloudTrail:

  1. Open the CloudTrail console and navigate to Event history.
  2. Select the AWS Region used for the integration.
  3. Filter events by Event source signin.amazonaws.com or Event name CreateOAuth2Token to locate OAuth token issuance activity.
  4. Review the event details, including the OAuth client identifier, target resource, authorization grant type, and token issuance status, where recorded.
  5. To review subsequent MCP activity, examine events from aws-mcp.amazonaws.com with the same session ARN and verify that the operations performed by the AI application match the permissions configured for the IAM role. Calls to global services such as IAM are recorded in US East (N. Virginia).

Example 1: AWS Sign-In OAuth token issuance

The following example illustrates the CloudTrail fields used to examine an OAuth token issuance event.

Best practices for securing AI agent access with EMA and AWS IAM

When configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA), consider the following security recommendations to help protect AI agent access to AWS resources:

  • Use short-lived ID-JAG assertions: Configure your enterprise IdP to issue ID-JAG assertions with short expiration periods. This limits the time during which an assertion can be exchanged for an OAuth access token and reduces the risk associated with token exposure.
  • Use tenant-specific IdP issuers: In multi-tenant environments, configure tenant-specific issuer URLs to establish explicit trust relationships between AWS and the intended enterprise IdP. This helps prevent assertions issued for one tenant from being accepted in another tenant’s authorization context.
  • Restrict OAuth authorization using IAM condition keys: Use IAM condition keys to limit OAuth token issuance to approved AI applications, authorization flows, and AWS resources. For example, use signin:OAuthClientId to restrict access to approved AI applications, such as arn:aws:signin:::external-client/jwt-bearer/anthropic-claude and signin:OAuthGrantType to restrict the permitted grant type to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. Scope these permissions to the AWS MCP Server service principal to prevent unintended access to other AWS services.
  • Apply least-privilege IAM permissions: Grant the IAM role only the permissions required by the AI application. Use managed policies to control which AWS operations the agent can perform through AWS MCP Server, reducing the impact of unauthorized or unintended actions.

For more information about available IAM condition keys and permissions, see the AWS Sign-In condition keys reference and the AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy documentation.

Conclusion

Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) with AWS Sign-In enables organizations to securely connect AI agents to AWS resources using their existing enterprise IdPs. By combining centralized authorization policies with IAM permissions, organizations can control which AI applications access their resources while reducing the need for employees to manage AWS credentials or complete additional authorization flows.

Using ID-JAG, AWS Sign-In exchanges enterprise-issued identity assertions for short-lived OAuth access tokens associated with IAM roles. This approach helps organizations enforce least-privilege access, reduce credential exposure, and simplify how employees securely access AWS resources through AI agents.

To get started, see the Sign-in with OAuth 2.0, Configure EMA for MCP servers, and Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server to learn more about OAuth-based access to AWS resources.

items.title: Reduce operational overhead by migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS
items.summary: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) supports the security certifications, algorithms, and performance that most AWS CloudHSM workloads require. Organizations that migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS have significantly reduced costs while eliminating hardware security module (HSM) provisioning, patching, and high-availability management. For a detailed comparison of both services, see AWS KMS or AWS CloudHSM: Choose the right key management solution . For payment workloads, see AWS Payment Cryptography in the following table. Is migration right for you? Most AWS CloudHSM workloads can migrate to AWS KMS. The following requirements might appear to need CloudHSM, but most have a resolution path: Potential requirement Resolution Contractual or compliance mandate requiring single-tenant HSMs Review your compliance documentation for explicit single-tenant language; many organizations find that it’s assumed, not mandated. Where mandated, a security review of AWS KMS typically confirms that its logical cryptographic isolation architecture satisfies the underlying intent. Applications that rely on traditional HSM interfaces (PKCS#11, Java Cryptography Extension, OpenSSL Provider, or Key Storage Provider) These interfaces are a communication pattern, not an architectural constraint. Contact your AWS account team to assess the refactoring effort needed for your workloads to use modern RESTful interfaces to web services. Deprecated algorithms (TDES, PKCS#1 v1.5 with RSA) or less common operations (AES key wrapping, AES-CTR, AES-CBC) Evaluate whether you can retire the dependency as part of your security modernization. Over 1 billion cryptographic operations per month, where higher per-operation AWS KMS costs might favor the per-hour AWS CloudHSM cost model Per-operation pricing is only one of several factors that affect cost. Also consider saved staff time, patching, and high-availability management. With envelope encryption (Option B in the following section), optional data key caching can further reduce API call volume. Payment workloads using older or payment-specific cryptography (TDES, AES-CBC) While AWS KMS embeds cryptographic best practices in a managed service, some payment systems still rely on older cryptography such as TDES. Evaluate Payment Cryptography, which supports payment use cases, including TDES-based algorithms such as CVV2, ARQC, and PIN validation. It also provides low-level algorithms, such as AES-CBC, that third-party systems might require for interoperability. If you can resolve these requirements, it’s possible to migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. You can use the rest of this post to review the basic steps of migration to AWS KMS. How migration works Migration has three parts: updating application code to call KMS APIs, rotating or importing your cryptographic keys, and transitioning existing data. You re-encrypt previously encrypted data under KMS keys, and existing signatures remain verifiable without AWS CloudHSM. You can complete each part gradually, with zero downtime. Application refactoring is the bulk of the effort, though AI-assisted code transformation tools can reduce this work. Because you’re already refactoring application code, this migration is also an opportunity to adopt post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms, discussed in the following section. Digital signature workloads During the transition, the AWS CloudHSM private key continues to sign existing workloads. If AWS CloudHSM lets you export (wrap) a copy of your private key, import it directly into AWS KMS to maintain continuity. For details, see How to Migrate Asymmetric Keys from CloudHSM to AWS KMS . If the key is non-exportable, create a new key pair in AWS KMS. A new asymmetric KMS key (or the imported key from CloudHSM) signs new data flowing to AWS KMS. Shift traffic from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS at your own pace. If you created a new key pair, export the CloudHSM public key before decommissioning and use it to verify existing signatures locally with libraries such as AWS-LC or OpenSSL as shown in Figure 1. AWS KMS doesn’t support importing public keys. Figure 1 – Digital signature migration Post-quantum readiness: When creating new signing keys in AWS KMS as part of this migration, consider adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC). AWS KMS supports ML-DSA (FIPS 204), so you can begin issuing PQC signatures now rather than as a separate future effort. This matters most for long-lived signatures, such as document signing, code signing, and certificate issuance. Durability of imported asymmetric keys: Asymmetric key material imported into AWS KMS (using ImportKeyMaterial ) doesn’t have the same durability guarantees as keys generated within AWS KMS. In the unlikely event of an AWS Region-wide infrastructure failure, imported key material could become unavailable. To protect against this, create the key as a multi-Region key, then import the same key material into each replica key in other Regions. Also keep secure backups of imported private keys outside of AWS KMS. An AWS CloudHSM cluster backup is a zero-cost option; CloudHSM stores backups in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at no additional charge. For keys created in AWS KMS (not imported), AWS KMS automatically manages durability within a Region, and multi-Region keys replicate the key material for you. Encryption workloads For encryption workloads, use the gradual re-encryption pattern: encrypt new data with AWS KMS while a background process re-encrypts existing data created under AWS CloudHSM keys. This achieves a zero-downtime migration. The following are two approaches to gradual re-encryption, depending on your requirements. Option A: Direct encryption with AWS KMS API (recommended) Call the AWS KMS Encrypt and Decrypt APIs directly (Figure 2). Your application passes plaintext to kms:Encrypt and receives a self-contained ciphertext blob. To decrypt, pass the blob to kms:Decrypt . There are no data keys to manage, no local cryptography, and no libraries beyond the AWS SDK. When decrypting, AWS KMS identifies the correct key from metadata it embeds in the ciphertext, including the key material identifier. As a result, ciphertext produced by AWS KMS is larger (by about 150 bytes) than AWS CloudHSM would produce for the same plaintext. During transition, your application must handle data encrypted by both systems. On decrypt, call kms:Decrypt first. If the ciphertext was created by kms:Encrypt , it will succeed. If it was created by CloudHSM, kms:Decrypt will return InvalidCiphertextException immediately without attempting decryption. Your application then falls back to the CloudHSM decrypt path and can optionally re-encrypt the plaintext with kms:Encrypt and store the new ciphertext. All new encrypt operations go to AWS KMS immediately; only decrypt needs the fallback until re-encryption is complete. The following pseudocode illustrates this pattern: def encrypt_record(record_id, record): response = kms.encrypt(KeyId=kms_key_arn, Plaintext=record) store(record_id, ciphertext=response['CiphertextBlob']) def decrypt_record(record_id): stored = fetch(record_id) try: response = kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=stored.ciphertext) return response['Plaintext'] except kms.exceptions.InvalidCiphertextException: # Not a KMS ciphertext - fall back to CloudHSM return cloudhsm_decrypt(stored.ciphertext) Figure 2 – Encryption migration with AWS KMS API More about AWS KMS encryption AWS KMS direct encryption supports plaintext up to 4 KB per request. For larger payloads, use Option B ( AWS Encryption SDK ), which handles envelope encryption for you and supports data of any size. AWS KMS also supports asymmetric encryption with RSA keys for use cases such as encrypting data destined for a specific key pair holder. This post focuses on symmetric encryption because it covers the majority of AWS CloudHSM encryption workloads. Option B: Envelope encryption with AWS Encryption SDK For workloads that require envelope encryption, use the AWS Encryption SDK as shown in Figure 3. Your application calls encrypt() on plaintext and decrypt() on ciphertext. The SDK manages data key generation, local 256-bit AES-GCM encryption, and serialization automatically. Its portable ciphertext format works across multiple runtimes of the AWS Encryption SDK. You can also enable data key caching to reduce calls to AWS KMS. Use this approach when you share encrypted data across services, languages, or with third parties outside of AWS. Figure 3 – Encryption migration with AWS Encryption SDK Migration results A financial services company migrated their transaction data encryption from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. Prior to migration, their workload ran 75 million cryptographic operations per month on three HSMs provisioned for high availability and the operational burden was 25 hours per month. After the migration, they no longer had to manage HSMs, which reduced their operational burden to near zero. Metric Before (AWS CloudHSM) After (AWS KMS) Monthly cost $3,456 (three HSMs) Approximately $250 (93% reduction) Operational burden 25 hours per month (patching, certificates, and monitoring) Near zero: no HSMs to manage Compliance FIPS 140-3 Level 3 FIPS 140-3 Level 3 Disaster recovery Multi-Availability Zone (AZ) HSMs that they provisioned, sized, and monitored Automatic multi-AZ availability. Optional multi-Region replication Migration duration – 10 weeks, zero downtime Recommendations We recommend the following as you migrate from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS. Use AI-assisted code transformation tools to accelerate refactoring and reduce manual effort. Run the complete migration in staging first, including re-encryption of representative data volumes. Document specific rollback criteria. During gradual re-encryption, you can pause at any point while AWS CloudHSM continues to decrypt data that has not yet moved. Keep KMS keys enabled after a rollback, because data already re-encrypted under AWS KMS still needs them. Design AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, key policies, grants, and encryption context schemas before migration. Encryption context enables fine-grained audit trails not available in CloudHSM. See the AWS KMS Developer Guide for a list of log entries. Delete CloudHSM keys only after all data is re-encrypted and verified. Before deleting, create a CloudHSM cluster backup of any keys imported into AWS KMS and export the public key of any signing key you replaced. Maintain an audit trail of the decommissioning. Next steps Start by auditing your current AWS CloudHSM usage: document your keys, the applications that use them, your monthly operation volume, and any compliance constraints. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate AWS KMS costs for your workload, then test a proof-of-concept migration with a non-critical application. Conclusion Migrating from AWS CloudHSM to AWS KMS removes the recurring work of provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring HSM clusters, freeing your team to focus on your application rather than the cryptographic infrastructure beneath it. You gain built-in high availability across multiple Availability Zones, with optional multi-Region replication, at a usage-based cost rather than a per-hour commitment for hardware you manage. Because the migration involves refactoring application code, it is also a natural point to adopt post-quantum signing algorithms such as ML-DSA, so you modernize your security posture in the same effort. For implementation support, contact your AWS account team or AWS Professional Services . For API integration details, see the AWS KMS Developer Guide . If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Derek Tumulak Derek Tumulak is a seasoned cybersecurity leader and Principal Product Manager at Amazon Web Services. With over 20 years of experience, he has held executive roles at Thales and Vormetric. A University of Waterloo graduate, Derek is a recognized expert in data security and encryption, frequently advising Silicon Valley organizations on advanced technical strategies and product innovation.

items.title: Chilling Effects: A Special Issue of the Virginia Journal of Law and Technology
items.summary: The Virginia Journal of Law and Technology (VJOLT) has published a special issue dedicated to senior research fellow Jon Penney’s new book Chilling Effects: Repression, Conformity, and Power in the Digital Age . The special issue brings together comments from a distinguished list of legal scholars inspired by Penney’s work on the growing weaponization of censorship, surveillance, and technology to control and repress. The Special Issue follows a VJOLT Symposium for the book held in February, which can be viewed here . Read here
