items.title: CVE-2026-123903: Critical VMware vCenter Authentication Bypass Requires Urgent Patching
items.summary: Broadcom has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-123903, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting VMware vCenter Server. The flaw resides in VMware Directory Service, or vmdir, and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical . A remote attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter deployment can exploit the weakness to bypass authentication and obtain unauthorized access without valid credentials or user interaction. Because vCenter acts as the centralized management layer for VMware virtual infrastructure, compromise of its identity and directory services can expose highly privileged administrative functionality. The vulnerability was disclosed on November 24, 2026 as part of VMSA-2026-0011, a broad security release addressing 23 flaws across VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, Tools, Cloud Foundation, and Avi Load Balancer. Broadcom credited researchers from QiAnXin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook with independently reporting the issue. CVE-2026-123903 is particularly notable because it follows CVE-2026-123890, another CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the same VMware Directory Service that was disclosed only days earlier and had already been exploited as a zero-day by the China-nexus ARMORY CASTLE group. Broadcom states that the two vulnerabilities are separate issues and should not be treated as the same attack path. Organizations can strengthen defenses against rapidly emerging infrastructure vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Contact Sales Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to transform vulnerability intelligence into hunting logic, refine detection rules, and adapt behavioral detections to the telemetry available across their VMware and broader infrastructure environments. Detect CVE-2026-123903 by monitoring unauthorized vCenter directory activity, anomalous administrative account creation, unusual authentication failures followed by privileged actions, and unexpected changes to SSO or Directory Service objects. CVE-2026-123903 analysis CVE-2026-123903 affects VMware vCenter deployments across multiple currently supported and legacy product branches, including vCenter 8.0, vCenter components included with VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 9.x, Cloud Foundation 5.x, and affected Telco Cloud products. Broadcom also lists vCenter 7.0 as affected, directing customers with extended support contracts to contact support for a fix. Broadcom describes the issue as an authentication bypass in VMware Directory Service. An attacker only requires network access to the vulnerable vCenter service; valid credentials and user interaction are not required. The CVSS vector is: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H This reflects remote accessibility, low attack complexity, no required privileges, and potentially high impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. VMware Directory Service provides core identity and directory functionality to vCenter. It stores and manages information used by VMware Single Sign-On and other identity-related components, making an authentication failure in this service particularly sensitive. Broadcom has not publicly documented the vulnerable function or exact protocol-level sequence required to trigger the bypass. Its official advisory states only that a network-accessible malicious actor can exploit the vulnerability to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access. However, public security research released after the advisory suggests that the issue may involve improper authentication-state handling during VMware Directory Service authentication. One publicly available repository claims that a failed SASL authentication sequence can leave authorization information associated with a connection, potentially allowing subsequent directory actions to execute with privileges that were never successfully authenticated. This technical interpretation has not been independently validated by Broadcom and should therefore be treated as public PoC research rather than vendor-confirmed exploit mechanics. The security implications of unauthorized Directory Service access can be substantial. vCenter controls virtual machines, ESXi hosts, storage, networking, role assignments, and identity relationships across a VMware environment. Depending on the privileges obtained after bypassing authentication, an attacker may be able to create or modify administrative identities, alter access controls, collect sensitive configuration information, or establish a foothold for broader virtualization infrastructure compromise. Organizations should avoid automatically assuming that CVE-2026-123903 provides direct code execution on ESXi hosts. Broadcom’s advisory confirms an authentication bypass and unauthorized system access, but it does not state that exploitation alone executes code on ESX or provides root-level command execution. This distinction is important because VMSA-2026-0011 also addresses separate ESX vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911, that can enable remote code execution on ESX hosts. Those vulnerabilities are different issues and should not be conflated with the vCenter authentication bypass. The CVE-2026-123903 PoC landscape developed rapidly after disclosure. At least one public GitHub repository appeared on November 24 claiming to demonstrate the VMware Directory Service authentication bypass. Public vulnerability trackers classify the repository as unvetted, and no Metasploit, Exploit-DB, or widely validated scanner module was identified at the time of writing. Broadcom has not reported exploitation in the wild. As of November 25, 2026, the vulnerability is also not listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The lack of confirmed attacks should not significantly reduce remediation priority because exploit information is already public and the flaw requires no valid account. The disclosure comes at a particularly sensitive time for VMware defenders. CVE-2026-123890, disclosed on November 19, affects the same Directory Service and had already been exploited by ARMORY CASTLE before patches became available. CVE-2026-123903 is explicitly described as a new and distinct issue, meaning organizations cannot assume that hunting guidance or indicators developed for the previous zero-day provide complete coverage for this vulnerability. For CVE-2026-123903 detection, defenders should focus on identity and directory behavior inside vCenter. Relevant signals include unexpected SSO administrator creation, unusual group membership changes, directory modifications without a corresponding successful login, and privileged actions originating from systems that do not normally administer VMware infrastructure. Security teams should also investigate authentication failures followed by successful directory activity over the same source connection or from the same source host. While Broadcom has not provided exploit-specific log signatures, this sequence may help identify attempts to manipulate authentication state. Network monitoring can add context by detecting unexpected access to vCenter management and directory services from user workstations, application servers, compromised Linux appliances, or other systems outside designated VMware management networks. Endpoint and appliance telemetry should be correlated with identity events. If suspicious vCenter authentication activity is followed by new users, configuration changes, SSH enablement, unexpected API activity, or access to ESXi systems, incident responders should treat the sequence as potentially malicious. Traditional CVE-2026-123903 IOCs such as attacker IP addresses, malware hashes, domains, or filenames have not been published by Broadcom because no confirmed attack campaign has been attributed to this vulnerability. Organizations should therefore prioritize behavior-based hunting and exposure assessment rather than waiting for campaign-specific indicators. Security teams looking for further details for CVE-2026-123903 should rely primarily on Broadcom’s VMSA-2026-0011 advisory and supplemental FAQ. Third-party PoCs may provide useful defensive context, but they should not be treated as authoritative descriptions of the vulnerability until independently validated. CVE-2026-123903 Mitigation Broadcom states that there is no workaround for the vulnerability. Installing a fixed vCenter release is therefore the primary remediation. The current fixed versions are: Product / Branch Fixed Version VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.1.x 9.1.2 VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation 9.0.x 9.0.2.0300 VMware vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter Server 7.0 Contact Broadcom under extended support VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform Follow Broadcom KB463501 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure Follow Broadcom KB463501 One operational nuance is especially important. Broadcom notes that security patches are cumulative, meaning some vulnerabilities in VMSA-2026-0011 were already corrected in earlier releases even though the response matrix lists the latest cumulative builds. For vCenter 8.0, 8.0 U3m is the fixed build listed for both the November 19 and November 24 security advisories. Organizations that already installed 8.0 U3m for CVE-2026-123890 are therefore on the build Broadcom lists as remediating the newer authentication bypass as well. By contrast, organizations running the VMware 9.x branches should verify their current build against the newer advisory rather than assuming last week’s security update remains sufficient. VMSA-2026-0011 lists 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300 as the current remediated versions. The most important CVE-2026-123903 mitigation step is therefore accurate version inventory followed by installation of the appropriate cumulative patch. Until patching is complete, organizations should reduce network exposure even though Broadcom does not list this as a formal workaround. vCenter should reside on a restricted management network and be reachable only from explicitly authorized administrative hosts, jump servers, and security tools. Direct internet exposure of vCenter management services should be avoided. Internal segmentation is equally important because attackers who compromise an endpoint, VPN appliance, remote support platform, or Linux infrastructure server may use that internal foothold to reach vCenter. Organizations should enforce least privilege for VMware administrative identities, remove unused SSO accounts, and monitor membership of high-privilege groups. Authentication bypasses reduce the value of password controls at the vulnerable boundary, but identity hardening can still limit persistence and follow-on abuse after remediation. After patching, security teams should perform a retrospective review of vCenter identity activity during the vulnerable period. Look for unexpected SSO accounts, administrative group changes, authentication anomalies, configuration modifications, and unusual API or management access. If unauthorized administrative access is identified, responders should not assume patch installation alone resolves the compromise. Potentially exposed credentials, API tokens, certificates, SSO accounts, and other authentication material should be reviewed and rotated where appropriate. Network access controls should also be reviewed to ensure VMware Directory Service and management interfaces are not broadly reachable across the enterprise. When was CVE-2026-123903 first discovered? The exact original discovery date has not been publicly disclosed. Broadcom credits researchers from QiAnXin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook with independently reporting the vulnerability. The issue was publicly disclosed through VMSA-2026-0011 on November 24, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-123903 on systems? Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated network attacker to bypass vCenter authentication and obtain unauthorized access to the system. Because vCenter controls identity, virtual machines, ESXi hosts, networking, and storage, privileged unauthorized access can create significant confidentiality, integrity, and availability risks. No official workaround exists. Restrict vCenter access to dedicated management networks, audit SSO administrator activity, and review systems that were exposed before patching for evidence of unauthorized directory or administrative changes.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Hex.pm Vulnerability to Execute Commands on Six Servers
items.summary: A critical Hex.pm vulnerability was exploited on November 23, 2026, allowing attackers to execute operating system commands on six web servers. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514, carries a maximum severity score of 10.0 and required no account. Hex blocked the attack and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. It found no evidence of package tampering but could not rule out access to user data. In its November 24 incident report, Hex said the attacker sent 69 malicious requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC. Investigators confirmed command execution by matching files created on the servers to request timestamps. A restart at 18:28 brought three more servers online with the vulnerable build, raising the total affected to six. All servers were running the patched build by 18:31 UTC. According to GitHub advisories , the Hex.pm flaw allowed attackers to exploit request decoding before authentication checks, using data crafted to resemble an internal Elixir structure. When the server tried to log an error involving that data, it treated the structure as trusted and ran commands with the application’s permissions. The patch rejects those structures during decoding. Hex traced the missing safety check back to February 2016. Critical Hex.pm Flaw Exploited The case shares a lesson with the Java4Shell decoder flaw : code that handles incoming data can expose a server before login checks run. But unlike the Shai-Hulud npm attack , Hex found no altered releases. Investigators matched all 23 releases published during the incident to audit records and verified 62 package files against stored checksums. Hex does not log database reads, so it could not determine whether the attacker viewed email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets, sessions, or audit logs. It also could not fully rule out access to private packages or documentation. Investigators found no evidence of unauthorized database changes or lasting access. Hex replaced storage, email, and database credentials, among others, and changed the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. That forced users to sign in again. Hex advises users to change their passwords and reset two-factor authentication in Dashboard → Security. Under Authenticator App, select “Setup New App,” verify a code from the new entry, and save the new recovery codes. Check that links in emails claiming to come from Hex lead to hex.pm and forward suspicious messages to security@hex.pm. ElixirForum advises downloading packages only from repo.hex.pm and avoiding third-party mirrors until Hex releases clients with the new registry-signing system. Once available, Mix users can update using mix local.hex --force . Developers using rebar3 or Gleam should update those tools as well. Hex’s investigation also uncovered a related issue in Ash, fixed in version 3.38.0. Projects using db_connection should upgrade to 2.10.3 or later. items.title: Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR): Turning Sigma Alerts into ATT&CK-Mapped Attack Chains
items.summary: Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR) are correlation rules that sit one level above standard Sigma detections. Instead of matching a single log event, a Higher Order Sigma rule links the Sigma rules that fire on one host into an attack chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Most SOC teams already run hundreds of Sigma rules. Higher Order Sigma Rules (HOSR) are correlation rules that sit one level above standard Sigma detections. Instead of matching a single log event, a Higher Order Sigma rule links the Sigma rules that fire on one host into an attack chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

Most SOC teams already run hundreds of Sigma rules. Each flags one suspicious step, such as an encoded PowerShell command or a new service install, but analysts still have to work out which alerts belong to the same intrusion. HOSR moves that reasoning into the detection content itself, so multi-stage attack detection starts before anyone opens the alert queue.

Contact Sales

What Is Higher Order Sigma?

Higher Order Sigma is a correlation layer for Sigma: rules whose inputs are the matches of other Sigma rules rather than raw events. SOC Prime introduced Higher Order Sigma rules in July 2026 and began a gradual rollout across its products.

Each Higher Order Sigma rule is built around an Active Threat, SOC Prime’s curated intelligence item on a current campaign or malware family. The rule takes the detection rules attached to that threat and orders them using the threat’s Attack Flow, a sequence of adversary techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The result describes how the whole attack unfolds, not just what one step looks like.

The name echoes higher-order functions in programming, which take other functions as input. A standard Sigma rule asks whether a suspicious event happened. A Higher Order Sigma rule asks whether the steps of a known attack are happening together, on the same machine or same user, within a short time.

In SOC Prime’s design, attack chains are authored by human experts as higher-order rules that correlate on ATT&CK techniques and on sequences of lower-level Sigma rules. Every rule is plain YAML, so detection engineers can read and review it like any other Sigma rule. 

How Does Standard Sigma Differ from Higher Order Sigma?

A standard Sigma rule checks one event against field conditions. A Higher Order Sigma rule checks a sequence of Sigma matches against an attack’s expected progression.

Standard Sigma is the vendor-agnostic YAML format detection engineers use to describe suspicious log events once and translate them to any SIEM, EDR, or data lake. Its strength is precision on a single log source. Its limit is that each rule sees one event in isolation, so ten related detections arrive as ten unrelated alerts.

The Sigma specification does offer correlation rules, such as event_count, value_count, temporal, and temporal_ordered, which group matches by a field within a timespan. They are useful, but each one is written by hand for a specific use case, and temporal types expect every referenced rule to match:

title: Admin share access followed by remote service install

correlation:

  type: temporal_ordered

  rules:

    – smb_admin_share_access

    – remote_service_creation

  group-by:

    – ComputerName

  timespan: 10m

If the attacker skips one step, a rule like this stays silent. Higher Order Sigma builds on the same correlation idea but is derived from threat intelligence, organized by ATT&CK stage, and designed to tolerate gaps.

AspectStandard Sigma ruleHigher Order Sigma ruleInputOne raw log eventEvents already tagged by Sigma rule matchesLogic sourceField conditions for one log sourceAttack Flow stages of an Active Threat, each backed by one or more Sigma rulesScopeA single eventMultiple events on the same host within a correlation windowMatchingExact: the condition is true or falsePartial: a chain forms once a set percentage of stages matchOutputA match tagged with ATT&CK technique and severityAn Attack Chain with match percentage, severity, and technique timelineWhere it runsSIEM, EDR, or pipeline queryCorrelation tier after Sigma tagging, in Prime Detect, Prime Hunt, and LogTotal

The two are complementary. Higher Order Sigma does not replace standard Sigma rules; it depends on them as building blocks.

What Are the Key Benefits for SOC Operations?

The main payoff is fewer, better alerts: analysts receive ATT&CK-mapped attack chains with context instead of isolated rule hits.

  • Less alert fatigue. Individual Sigma matches become tags, not alerts, and only correlated chains reach the queue. The funnel is steep: roughly 7% of raw events get tagged, and only a tiny fraction of those tagged events ever form an attack chain worth alerting on.
  • Fewer false positives. One noisy rule cannot create a chain on its own; it needs corroborating steps on the same host. An AI agent then classifies each chain as a confirmed detection or a likely false positive, and filtered-out chains are hidden by default.
  • Resilience to partial evasion. Because chains form at a match threshold, an attacker who skips a step or evades one rule can still be caught. At a 50% threshold, three of six stages are enough.
  • Faster triage. Each Attack Chain arrives with an AI summary, a technique timeline, and the matched rules, so analysts start from the full story instead of rebuilding it.
  • Less rule tuning. Because a single rule match no longer triggers an alert, noisy rules cost far less. Fine-tuning shifts from rewriting rules to adding context, which an AI agent can apply on top of the correlation output.
  • ATT&CK-aligned reporting. Every chain carries techniques, sub-techniques, and related threat actors, which feeds coverage reporting and threat-informed defense directly.
How Does Higher Order Sigma Work?

Higher Order Sigma is the second tier of a three-tier correlation process: Sigma rules tag events, Higher Order Sigma rules chain them, and an AI agent triages the result.

  1. Tier 1: Sigma rules tag events. In Prime Detect, Sigma rules run on streaming data before it reaches the SIEM, and each match carries an ATT&CK technique and a severity. In Prime Hunt, Sigma rules are translated into native queries and run against your Data Plane, whether SIEM, EDR/XDR, or data lake. Either way, a match marks an event as relevant; it is not yet an alert.
  2. Tier 2: Higher Order Sigma rules evaluate the sequence. Each rule maps to an Active Threat, and its stages follow that threat’s Attack Flow. A stage counts as matched when any of its underlying Sigma rules fires. Tagged events are grouped by host within the correlation window, and an Attack Chain forms once the matched stages reach the configured threshold.
  3. Tier 3: An AI agent triages the chain. The agent enriches the chain with context, analyzes the event sequence, and classifies it as a confirmed detection or a likely false positive.
  4. Analysts investigate and respond. Each chain moves through a status lifecycle, from New and Investigating to Confirmed or False Positive, then Resolved or Closed.

For example, imagine an Active Threat whose Attack Flow has six stages, from initial execution through credential dumping to lateral movement. With a 50% threshold, Sigma matches for any three of those stages on the same host, inside the correlation window, form an Attack Chain with a 50% match score. A single matching stage stays a quiet tag.

The same correlation powers LogTotal, SOC Prime’s tool for investigating logs during an incident. It matches exported logs against detection rules, then uses Higher Order Sigma rules and agentic AI to return ranked attack chains.

Conclusion

Higher Order Sigma Rules shift detection from “what happened” to “which attack is in progress.” For SOC teams, that means fewer and richer alerts, ATT&CK-mapped attack chains, and detection logic that tolerates gaps. To explore them, open any Active Threat on the SOC Prime Platform and check its Higher Order Sigma tab, or filter Advanced Search by Higher Order Sigma.

items.title: Introducing Search for Agents
items.summary: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. How it works The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). Discoverability Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site. For example, for HTML responses, we add metadata to the page's : If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting a page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter: --- agent: instructions: "Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown." endpoint: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}" method: "GET" documentation: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/" --- The agent will easily pick up these instructions and know what to do next to search your site. Searching content Once the agent knows that your site has a search endpoint, it can start using it: $ curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts" # Search results for: "cloudflare artifacts" ## docs/artifacts/api/workers-binding/index.md (score: 1.000) # Workers binding · Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Call Artifacts from a Worker binding. --- ## docs/artifacts/index.md (score: 0.951) # Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Store, version, and share filesystem artifacts across Workers, APIs, and Git-compatible tools. ... Depending on your AI Search configuration, the agent can also use natural language and ask questions to the search endpoint: $ curl --get "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search" --data-urlencode "q=What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" # Search results for: "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" ## docs/artifacts/platform/limits/index.limits-cloudflare-artifacts-docs.md (score: 1.000) # Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Section: Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs title: Limits description: Review Artifacts platform limits. pcx_content_type: reference products: - artifacts Limits that apply to creating, importing, cloning, and pushing Artifacts are detailed below. These limits cover naming rules, storage, request rates for control-plane and Git operations, and the size of each push. FeatureLimitControl-plane request rate2,000 requests per 10 seconds per Artifacts namespaceGit request rate, per artifact2,000 requests per 10 seconds per artifactMaximum storage per repository1 GB for repos created on or after 2026-09-29. Repos created earlier have a 10 GB limit. See size limit change.Maximum storage per account1 TB (can be raised on request)Maximum number of repositoriesUnlimitedMaximum number of namespacesUnlimitedNamespace name length2–63 charactersNamespace and repo namesStart with a letter or digit. Remaining characters may include letters, digits, ., _, and -.Maximum push size64 MiB per push. Includes all data sent in the push. Split larger work into several smaller pushes.Maximum objects per push50,000 objects, such as file versions, folders, and commits.Maximum file size32 MiB per file. Already-compressed files, like images, video, or zip archives, may be rejected slightly below 32 MiB.Maximum ref updates per push1 MiB of branch and tag updates per push.Maximum entries per folder100,000 files and subfolders in a single folder. ... Note that this search endpoint returns retrieved content, in Markdown, not a generated answer. The agent already has an AI model and a conversation with the user; all it needs is the relevant information from your site, not another AI model's attempt to answer on its behalf. Supporting a new HTTP method: QUERY The new HTTP QUERY method is an IETF Proposed Standard, incidentally coauthored by our own James Snell , published in June 2026 as RFC 10008 . A QUERY allows a client to send search criteria in a request body safely and idempotently without modifying server state. This makes it a good fit for AI search. The adoption of QUERY is underway with major browser vendors discussing the RFC and multiple frameworks and clients either adopting ( curl and undici , for example), or discussing adoption. Search for Agents supports QUERY natively either using a plain text or JSON request body: # Plain text curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?' # JSON curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}' See it in action Let’s see it in action during an agentic session. Search for Agents is enabled for our Developer Documentation . When we open an OpenCode session and ask “What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?”, in the logs we can see the agent discovering the search endpoint on the homepage and then fetching /.well-known/search with the question for the search results. The answer comes back a few seconds later and it’s correct. Once the agent discovers the search API, it will likely reuse it multiple times within the same session whenever it needs to search for content in the same site. We enabled Search for Agents for our developer documentation ahead of this announcement and we’ve found that agents do a good job of discovering the search API and using it during their tasks. It’s still an AI Search instance Because Search for Agents is powered by an AI Search instance in your account, you get all the standard configuration options and features as well. For example, you can enable public REST API or MCP endpoints, or use it from Workers , or even embed AI Search on your website for human visitors. Start using Search for Agents Starting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers. The usage follows the AI Search pricing ; that includes ingesting content, storing the index's content, and serving queries, subject to the account's included usage and limits for both the Workers Free and Paid plans. We also recommend you check our Agent Readiness page (see announcement ) and understand how you can make your sites optimized for agents, from guiding agents on how to authenticate, to controlling what content agents can see, the format they receive it in, and how they pay for it. Check out the Search for Agents developer docs for more information. Follow us on X or come and talk to us in the Cloudflare Developer Discord . We'd like to hear from site owners making their content searchable to agents.

Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall (WAF) configurations).

Discoverability

Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site.

For example, for HTML responses, we add metadata to the page's :

If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting a page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter:

---
agent:
  instructions: "Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown."
  endpoint: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}"
  method: "GET"
  documentation: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/"
---

The agent will easily pick up these instructions and know what to do next to search your site.

Searching content

Once the agent knows that your site has a search endpoint, it can start using it:

$ curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts"
# Search results for: "cloudflare artifacts"

Depending on your AI Search configuration, the agent can also use natural language and ask questions to the search endpoint:

Note that this search endpoint returns retrieved content, in Markdown, not a generated answer. The agent already has an AI model and a conversation with the user; all it needs is the relevant information from your site, not another AI model's attempt to answer on its behalf.

Supporting a new HTTP method: QUERY

The new HTTP QUERY method is an IETF Proposed Standard, incidentally coauthored by our own James Snell, published in June 2026 as RFC 10008. A QUERY allows a client to send search criteria in a request body safely and idempotently without modifying server state. This makes it a good fit for AI search.

curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \

When we open an OpenCode session and ask “What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?”, in the logs we can see the agent discovering the search endpoint on the homepage and then fetching /.well-known/search with the question for the search results.

Once the agent discovers the search API, it will likely reuse it multiple times within the same session whenever it needs to search for content in the same site.

We enabled Search for Agents for our developer documentation ahead of this announcement and we’ve found that agents do a good job of discovering the search API and using it during their tasks.

items.title: GitHub Enterprise Server is now available on SonarQube Cloud
items.summary: Organizations running GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) no longer have to choose between staying self-hosted and getting modern, cloud-delivered code verification. SonarQube Cloud's native integration with GitHub Enterprise Server is now generally available (GA) in the EU and US regions. Until now, deep GitHub-native verification was something GHES customers associated with SonarQube Server. With this release, that same hands-off, automated experience that GitHub.com customers already use with SonarQube Cloud is now available to enterprises running GitHub on their own infrastructure. What changed: from allowlist to GA Previously, connecting a self-hosted GHES instance to SonarQube Cloud required requesting allowlist access from SonarSource and relying on a preview integration without a committed support posture. That friction is gone. With GA: Enterprise administrators no longer need to contact SonarSource to request allowlist access. GHES connects the same way any other generally available platform does. Public documentation confirms GHES as a generally available, production-ready integration, so evaluation and procurement no longer depend on a status check with SonarSource. GHES incidents are now handled at the same severity and response priority as every other GA platform integration. On-call engineers supporting SonarQube Cloud's platform integrations treat GHES issues with the same urgency as GitHub.com, GitLab, or BitBucket incidents. In short, GHES is no longer a special case. It is a first-class, fully supported platform in SonarQube Cloud. What's included in this release Direct organization binding in supported regions Enterprise administrators can now bind their GHES organizations directly to SonarQube Cloud, with support for both EU and US regions. This gives organizations with regional data residency or compliance requirements a clear, supported path to connect their self-hosted GitHub instance without routing around infrastructure constraints. Analysis for private and internal repositories SonarQube Cloud now analyzes private and internal GHES repositories, not just public ones. This matters because the majority of enterprise codebases running on GHES are private by design. Full coverage means your verification layer extends to the code your organization actually ships, not a subset of it. Pull request decoration Quality and security results now surface directly in pull requests on GHES, the same way they do for GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHEC). Developers see issues where they already work, in the PR, rather than having to leave their workflow to check a separate dashboard. That keeps verification inside the review process instead of adding a step after it. Bulk import with automatic onboarding Instead of connecting repositories one at a time, administrators can import GHES repositories in bulk. Imported repositories get automatic main branch analysis out of the box, and new repositories created after the initial import are onboarded automatically. For platform teams managing hundreds or thousands of repositories, this removes a significant source of manual setup and the configuration drift that comes with it. Quality gate enforcement in GHES pipelines quality gates now enforce directly in GHES CI/CD pipelines, giving teams a deterministic pass/fail checkpoint before code merges. Verification becomes a gate in the pipeline itself, not a report that is generated after code has already shipped. Full feature parity with GHEC This release brings GHES to functional parity with the existing GitHub Enterprise Cloud integration. That includes lines of code (LOC) consumption tracking, webhooks, and API access, all working the same way they do today for GHEC organizations. Teams that already operate SonarQube Cloud workflows against GHEC do not need to learn a second set of behaviors to support GHES. Who this is for This release is built for enterprise organizations that run GitHub Enterprise Server for security, compliance, or infrastructure control reasons, and that want the same verification experience available to GitHub.com and GHEC customers. It is relevant to: Enterprise administrators who manage self-hosted GHES instances and need a GA-supported integration path, not a preview or allowlist exception. Platform engineering teams responsible for onboarding and maintaining analysis coverage across large repository fleets. Security and compliance teams that require regional data residency guarantees and consistent, auditable verification across private and internal repositories. On-call and site reliability teams supporting SonarQube Cloud, who now treat GHES with the same incident severity as every other GA platform. If your organization previously evaluated SonarQube Cloud for GHES and stopped because of allowlist requirements or an unclear support status, that blocker no longer applies. For a full technical walkthrough, see the GHES integration documentation .

  • GHES incidents are now handled at the same severity and response priority as every other GA platform integration. On-call engineers supporting SonarQube Cloud's platform integrations treat GHES issues with the same urgency as GitHub.com, GitLab, or BitBucket incidents.

In short, GHES is no longer a special case. It is a first-class, fully supported platform in SonarQube Cloud.

What's included in this releaseDirect organization binding in supported regions

Enterprise administrators can now bind their GHES organizations directly to SonarQube Cloud, with support for both EU and US regions. This gives organizations with regional data residency or compliance requirements a clear, supported path to connect their self-hosted GitHub instance without routing around infrastructure constraints.

Analysis for private and internal repositories

SonarQube Cloud now analyzes private and internal GHES repositories, not just public ones. This matters because the majority of enterprise codebases running on GHES are private by design. Full coverage means your verification layer extends to the code your organization actually ships, not a subset of it.

Pull request decoration

Quality and security results now surface directly in pull requests on GHES, the same way they do for GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHEC). Developers see issues where they already work, in the PR, rather than having to leave their workflow to check a separate dashboard. That keeps verification inside the review process instead of adding a step after it.

Bulk import with automatic onboarding

Instead of connecting repositories one at a time, administrators can import GHES repositories in bulk. Imported repositories get automatic main branch analysis out of the box, and new repositories created after the initial import are onboarded automatically. For platform teams managing hundreds or thousands of repositories, this removes a significant source of manual setup and the configuration drift that comes with it.

Quality gate enforcement in GHES pipelines

quality gates now enforce directly in GHES CI/CD pipelines, giving teams a deterministic pass/fail checkpoint before code merges. Verification becomes a gate in the pipeline itself, not a report that is generated after code has already shipped.

Full feature parity with GHEC

This release brings GHES to functional parity with the existing GitHub Enterprise Cloud integration. That includes lines of code (LOC) consumption tracking, webhooks, and API access, all working the same way they do today for GHEC organizations. Teams that already operate SonarQube Cloud workflows against GHEC do not need to learn a second set of behaviors to support GHES.

Who this is for

This release is built for enterprise organizations that run GitHub Enterprise Server for security, compliance, or infrastructure control reasons, and that want the same verification experience available to GitHub.com and GHEC customers. It is relevant to:

  • Enterprise administrators who manage self-hosted GHES instances and need a GA-supported integration path, not a preview or allowlist exception.
  • Platform engineering teams responsible for onboarding and maintaining analysis coverage across large repository fleets.
  • Security and compliance teams that require regional data residency guarantees and consistent, auditable verification across private and internal repositories.
  • On-call and site reliability teams supporting SonarQube Cloud, who now treat GHES with the same incident severity as every other GA platform.

If your organization previously evaluated SonarQube Cloud for GHES and stopped because of allowlist requirements or an unclear support status, that blocker no longer applies.

For a full technical walkthrough, see the GHES integration documentation.

New York vs auto-enshittification ( permalink ) As of February 27, 2027, it will be illegal for companies in New York to charge car-owners a subscription fee or an upcharge for any software feature that runs on hardware already installed in their car. It's a bold – if imperfect – disenshittification gambit aimed at the extremely (and increasingly) enshittified automotive industry: https://wgna.com/car-bill-extra-fees/ In a state of nature, there'd be no reason to pass a law like this. Say BMW decided to sell you a car that charged you a monthly subscription for the "feature" that auto-dipped your high-beams when there was an oncoming car (a thing BMW actually does): https://www.autoevolution.com/news/netizens-up-in-arms-over-bmw-adaptive-headlight-subscription-237335.html In a state of nature, BMW's sleazy scam would conjure forth competitors who would offer mechanics and drivers a one-click way to unlock the feature forever. Drivers would curse BMW and pay a one-time fee to get permanent access to the feature, and that would be the end of the matter. Indeed, the fact that this third-party fix could exist at all might well convince BMW not to bother with the high-beam scam in the first place (and if it didn't, well, then tinkerers, hackers, and entrepreneurs would swiftly obviate it). But we don't live in a state of nature. We live in a world with a federal "anticircumvention" law: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA 1201), which imposes a 5-year sentence and a $500k fine for this kind of reverse engineering, even if it does not result in a copyright infringement. There's no copyright law that says you can't change the software in your car to activate your high-beams' automatic controller, but that doesn't matter, because activating the controller without BMW's permission requires a reverse-engineering step and that's a felony. Jay Freeman rightly calls this "felony contempt of business model" because it lets companies send you to literal prison for doing otherwise legal things, just because it makes them unhappy. What's more, copyright is a firmly federal matter: copyright law "pre-empts" the states, meaning that states can't pass laws that modify federal copyright policy. That means that states can't override DMCA 1201 by legalizing reverse-engineering for otherwise lawful purposes (such as independent repair, performing software upgrades, or allowing generic consumables and parts). Anticircumvention is an attractive nuisance: it invites manufacturers to dream up as many scams as they can think of and then bury them in their products, secure in the knowledge that it is a literal felony to thwart their commercial plans. It's especially bad for cars, where anticircumvention is used: to block third-party parts and independent repair; to prevent drivers from preventing manufacturers, lenders and dealerships from spying on their driving habits, car informatics, and locations; to enable lenders (and hackers who break into dealerships' computers) to immobilize your car without any notice, appeal or due process: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/24/rent-to-pwn/#kitt-is-a-demon The New York State bill (S.9348A/A.10411A) partially addresses some of these unfair and deceptive practices: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A Before I get into what this law does (and doesn't) do, I want to get into how it does anything at all . Remember: anticircumvention was shoehorned into copyright law, and copyright is a federal matter. Copyright enjoys pre-emption, a ban on states' modifying it. At first blush, it seems like the states shouldn't be able to do anything about the enshittification that anticircumvention law enables. But the Right to Repair movement came up with a clever hack around pre-emption. States can't override federal copyright law, but state legislatures can regulate goods and services that are sold within their states. That means that states can simply ban the sale of goods that use anticircumvention to rip off or spy on the people who live within state limits. This is the basis for several successful Right to Repair laws, starting in 2022 with Colorado's powered wheelchair repair law (HB22-1031, cosponsored by the very excellent Brianna Titone): https://pluralistic.net/2022/06/08/chair-ish/#r2r This law does not purport to limit which copyrights the private-equity-backed powered wheelchair duopoly can exercise. It just orders anyone selling powered wheelchairs in Colorado to take steps to enable independent repair such that these copyright issues (including anticircumvention) never arise. This became the template for a slew of state repair bills, including Oregon's electronics repair law, which was later copy/pasted into Washington state law: https://pirg.org/oregon/updates/governor-kotek-signs-the-right-to-repair-act-into-law/ A very similar law was passed in New York state, only to be gutted by Governor Kathy Hochul: https://www.techdirt.com/2024/02/07/nys-right-to-repair-law-was-neutered-by-lobbyists-and-governor-hochul-after-passage-now-some-lawmakers-are-trying-to-fix-it/ Hochul will shortly get a chance to redeem herself, when A8405, a law that re-inserts all the provisions she stripped out of the original repair law, comes to her desk: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A8405 Perhaps Hochul will sign that law. After all, her press release about the new automotive bill sure makes it sound like she's anti-enshittification: My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets. https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription But the specifics of this new NY automotive bill matter, and they're a decidedly mixed bag. Let's start with the penalty for noncompliance: a dealer, automotive manufacturer or lender who violates the new law faces a whopping $250 fine per violation. That means that if your dealer charges you $1,000 for a software upgrade and you later realize you've been ripped off, they'll only pay a penalty of $250. In this case, a dealer who manages to fleece one driver for every three who know their rights and can figure out how to enforce them will still come out ahead – and that's only if you can get the dealer to refund your $1000, which might involve going to small claims court. Then there's the carve-outs: this law does not cover subscription fees and software upsells for "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle wi-fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This is a huge loophole. Take that last clause, "services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This clause allows manufacturers to bypass the entire statute, merely by redesigning their subscription and software upsells to "rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." For example, the BMW feature that automatically dips your high-beams could "require" a daily check for new versions and then the company can claim that the feature relies "on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." Sure, a judge might eventually find that "continued operation" doesn't mean a daily check for software updates, but only after the state AG or a class action lawyer forces the question, which could take years. Also: don't hold your breath waiting for the class action lawyer, because the car manufacturers can also make you click through a binding arbitration waiver when you first turn on your car and thus take away your right to join a class action: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/27/shit-shack/#binding-arbitration Beyond this, there's the breadth of vague phrases like "driver automation features" (is automatically dipping your high-beams a "driver automation feature?" I could sure see a lawyer making that argument). Likewise "telematics" (a buzzword that might mean anything, nothing or everything). On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see! Like I said, this is only a partial fix for auto-enshittification. It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer: https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car: https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill. Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad. It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification. But none of this should be necessary at all , and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see!

Like I said, this is only a partial fix for auto-enshittification. It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars

It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based

It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world

This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill.

Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad.

It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification.

But none of this should be necessary at all, and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

items.title: 🚀 The story behind “Drone 2”: My KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 keynote
items.summary: An open source adventure featuring Kubernetes, agent-substrate, kagent, AI agents, drones, and more! Just 30 seconds before going live for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 closing keynote, “Cloud Native Without Limits: What Can AI Agents Do for Us?”, while Abdel Sghiouar was introducing me, Cory Jett leaned over and whispered: “The drone isn’t connecting to the controller!” 😱 A heart-stopping moment! Thankfully, a quick reboot saved the day. And then came the moment I’ll never forget: walking onto the stage with a live drone following right behind me! 🚁✨ And when I finally walked off stage, all the nervousness and anxiety were gone. I was just SO happy! What a feeling! ❤️ On-stage live demo with the drone and big screens 🥋 From Amsterdam to Salt Lake City: Never give up! After my Amsterdam keynote , where the drone camera failed, Christian Dussol taught me the martial arts lesson of “Osu” (never give up! 🥋💪). That lesson stuck with me, and I wanted to push the boundaries even further in Salt Lake City. Striking the “Osu” posture after the Amsterdam keynote While brainstorming with Allison Price around our theme, “Cloud Native Without Limits,” we asked ourselves: What if we could let the audience experience what it’s like to fly and build something live on stage, powered by AI agents? Of course, bringing a live drone indoors isn’t exactly plug-and-play. There was quite a bit of work behind the scenes! 🛠️ Behind the scenes: Making the impossible possible A few challenges we had to tackle: 🛩️ Regulatory compliance: Back in August, we learned that an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot was required for our indoor drone operation. Cory stepped up, completed the necessary training in just one week, and saved the demo! 🙌 Teaser at the venue 😅 🏠 Home testing: I got propeller guards so I could safely experiment with code, test flight paths, and practice flying indoors at home. Let’s just say my house became a mini drone testing lab! Flight testing at home with propeller guards But this demo was about much more than flying a drone. We wanted to show what real-time agentic execution looks like, with the right guardrails, sandboxing, and observability in place. 🤖 Under the hood: The Cloud Native technologies behind the drone Here’s what powered the experience: 🤖 Agents: Running on CNCF Sanbox projects agent-substrate , and kagent providing an opinionated layer for building and running agents. 🔐Then AAIF Growth project agentgateway : Playing multiple roles: LLM gateway: Rate limiting and controlling access to models. Egress gateway (as part of agent-substrate): Enforcing sandbox and network access policies. MCP gateway: Handling authentication and authorization for Model Context Protocol tool calls with an Identity Provider, for example, Keycloak. 📊 OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: Providing end-to-end observability across agent execution through agentgateway and agent-substrate, including rate-limiting errors, the duration of each tool call, and where agents spend most of their time. All coming together to make an AI-powered physical experience happen, live on stage! The moment when it all comes together live on stage 💜 A big Thank You & what’s next? 🇪🇸 The community’s response was incredible! It’s exciting to see how far we’ve come as an industry, bringing AI models, agentic AI, and cloud native technologies together to make things possible that would have seemed like science fiction just a few years ago. A massive THANK YOU to my manager, Idit Levine , for her unwavering support; Cory Jett , for making the drone flight possible; Allison Price , for brainstorming this adventure with me; Jonathan Bryce , for loving the drone idea when I casually brought it up during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2025; Elna Vogel , for making sure we had the required insurance. And of course, a huge shout-out to the entire event and technical teams who helped bring this adventure to life! ❤️ Last but definitely not least, THANK YOU to the agent-substrate, kagent, and agentgateway communities! They answered every question I threw at them, responded incredibly quickly, and were always ready to jump in and debug live if needed. I couldn’t have pulled this off without you! 💜 My #substrate-dev team CNCF slack 📺 Missed the keynote? Catch the full recording! Now, I’m officially wrapping up the Drone 2 chapter and already looking forward to building something fresh for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2027 in Barcelona! 🇪🇸 So, what physical objects or hardware should we hack on next? Drones have had their moment. What’s next? What could we build that I haven’t even imagined yet? 🙂
items.summary_html:
An open source adventure featuring Kubernetes, agent-substrate, kagent, AI agents, drones, and more!

Just 30 seconds before going live for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 closing keynote, “Cloud Native Without Limits: What Can AI Agents Do for Us?”, while Abdel Sghiouar was introducing me, Cory Jett leaned over and whispered: “The drone isn’t connecting to the controller!” 😱

A heart-stopping moment!

Thankfully, a quick reboot saved the day. And then came the moment I’ll never forget: walking onto the stage with a live drone following right behind me! 🚁✨

And when I finally walked off stage, all the nervousness and anxiety were gone. I was just SO happy! What a feeling! ❤️

On-stage live demo with the drone and big screens

🥋 From Amsterdam to Salt Lake City: Never give up!

After my Amsterdam keynote, where the drone camera failed, Christian Dussol taught me the martial arts lesson of “Osu” (never give up! 🥋💪). That lesson stuck with me, and I wanted to push the boundaries even further in Salt Lake City.

Striking the “Osu” posture after the Amsterdam keynote

While brainstorming with Allison Price around our theme, “Cloud Native Without Limits,” we asked ourselves: What if we could let the audience experience what it’s like to fly and build something live on stage, powered by AI agents?

Of course, bringing a live drone indoors isn’t exactly plug-and-play. There was quite a bit of work behind the scenes!

🛠️ Behind the scenes: Making the impossible possible

A few challenges we had to tackle:

🛩️ Regulatory compliance: Back in August, we learned that an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot was required for our indoor drone operation. Cory stepped up, completed the necessary training in just one week, and saved the demo! 🙌

Teaser at the venue 😅

🏠 Home testing: I got propeller guards so I could safely experiment with code, test flight paths, and practice flying indoors at home. Let’s just say my house became a mini drone testing lab!

Flight testing at home with propeller guards

But this demo was about much more than flying a drone. We wanted to show what real-time agentic execution looks like, with the right guardrails, sandboxing, and observability in place.

🤖 Under the hood: The Cloud Native technologies behind the drone

Here’s what powered the experience:

🤖 Agents: Running on CNCF Sanbox projects agent-substrate, and kagent providing an opinionated layer for building and running agents.

🔐Then AAIF Growth project agentgateway: Playing multiple roles:

  • LLM gateway: Rate limiting and controlling access to models.
  • Egress gateway (as part of agent-substrate): Enforcing sandbox and network access policies.
  • MCP gateway: Handling authentication and authorization for Model Context Protocol tool calls with an Identity Provider, for example, Keycloak.

📊 OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: Providing end-to-end observability across agent execution through agentgateway and agent-substrate, including rate-limiting errors, the duration of each tool call, and where agents spend most of their time.

All coming together to make an AI-powered physical experience happen, live on stage!

The moment when it all comes together live on stage

💜 A big Thank You & what’s next? 🇪🇸

The community’s response was incredible! It’s exciting to see how far we’ve come as an industry, bringing AI models, agentic AI, and cloud native technologies together to make things possible that would have seemed like science fiction just a few years ago.

A massive THANK YOU to my manager, Idit Levine, for her unwavering support; Cory Jett, for making the drone flight possible; Allison Price, for brainstorming this adventure with me; Jonathan Bryce, for loving the drone idea when I casually brought it up during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2025; Elna Vogel, for making sure we had the required insurance.

And of course, a huge shout-out to the entire event and technical teams who helped bring this adventure to life! ❤️

Last but definitely not least, THANK YOU to the agent-substrate, kagent, and agentgateway communities! They answered every question I threw at them, responded incredibly quickly, and were always ready to jump in and debug live if needed. I couldn’t have pulled this off without you! 💜

My #substrate-dev team CNCF slack

📺 Missed the keynote? Catch the full recording!

Now, I’m officially wrapping up the Drone 2 chapter and already looking forward to building something fresh for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2027 in Barcelona! 🇪🇸

So, what physical objects or hardware should we hack on next? Drones have had their moment. What’s next? What could we build that I haven’t even imagined yet? 🙂

Some files were labeled “US” A separate database held 840 million Chinese ID numbers and 11 million student records If you suspect malware, use a clean device to change affected passwords and sign out everywhere Two unsecured databases have exposed billions of records, ranging from passwords and browser cookies to national ID numbers and children’s school details. Researchers discovered the databases separately, and the two appear to be unrelated. Both illustrate how personal information from different sources can end up together in a searchable collection. Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the larger database, which contained approximately 2 billion login records spread across 8,471 folders. Some files were labeled by country, including the US, though it’s unclear how many US residents were affected. The database required no password to access and stored credentials and account details in plaintext. Fowler reported that the exposed material included: Email addresses, usernames, passwords, and associated login URLs. Browser cookies, session tokens, and other authentication information. Saved application credentials and browser data. Device and operating-system information. Logs that appeared to contain autofill information and cryptocurrency wallet data. Fowler also identified approximately 400,000 documents that appeared to come from malware capable of creating more detailed collections about individual victims. That makes this more than a list of passwords. Some of the material could help an attacker connect a person’s accounts, identify their device, and potentially access an account where the person was already signed in. Fowler could not identify the database’s owner. He notified its hosting provider, and public access was restricted several days later. How long it had been exposed, and whether anyone else accessed it, remain unknown. In the separate discovery, researcher Greg Pollock identified an Elasticsearch server exposing approximately 259 GB of data on people in mainland China. Anyone who knew its address could search it without a password. Its 99 indices contained almost 1.64 billion records linking names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, student information, and business registrations. These included at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers and about 11 million student enrollment records. Some student records linked a child’s name to their school, class, and a parent’s contact details. This database brought together information from identity registration, education, telecommunications, payment, and business systems. Based on how the records were organized, UpGuard believes someone combined them to create an illicit identity-lookup service. Pollock could not identify the operator. During his investigation, the server became inaccessible, apparently following a ransomware or other destructive attack. Other copies of the data may still exist. Are your details being used by cybercriminals? FIND OUT HERE How to stay safe If malware stole your login details, changing affected passwords is a good start. Use a clean device to make those changes, and sign out of existing sessions in case someone also has the cookies that keep you logged in. Check for infection. Run a scan with a trusted anti-malware product . If you suspect an active infostealer infection, disconnect the affected device and use a separate, clean device for urgent account recovery. Otherwise, malware could capture replacement passwords too. Secure your most important accounts first . Start with your primary email, followed by banking, payment, work, and other sensitive accounts. Replace exposed or reused passwords with unique ones, using a password manager to generate and store them. Enable multifactor authentication . An authenticator app or security key adds protection against someone signing in with a stolen password. Sign out existing sessions. Look in your account’s security settings for an option such as “sign out everywhere,” “log out of all devices,” or “revoke active sessions.” Removing malware and changing passwords do not necessarily stop someone using an already stolen session token. Watch for financial and identity misuse. Review account activity and credit reports for transactions or accounts you don’t recognize. Review unsolicited messages with extra care. If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard . It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next. You can replace a password. Details like the school you attended can stay useful to scammers for years. If an unexpected caller or message mentions something personal, verify who you’re dealing with before sharing information or sending money. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

In this article

  • A separate database held 840 million Chinese ID numbers and 11 million student records
  • If you suspect malware, use a clean device to change affected passwords and sign out everywhere

Two unsecured databases have exposed billions of records, ranging from passwords and browser cookies to national ID numbers and children’s school details. Researchers discovered the databases separately, and the two appear to be unrelated. Both illustrate how personal information from different sources can end up together in a searchable collection.

Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered the larger database, which contained approximately 2 billion login records spread across 8,471 folders. Some files were labeled by country, including the US, though it’s unclear how many US residents were affected. The database required no password to access and stored credentials and account details in plaintext.

Fowler reported that the exposed material included:

  • Email addresses, usernames, passwords, and associated login URLs.
  • Browser cookies, session tokens, and other authentication information.
  • Saved application credentials and browser data.
  • Device and operating-system information.
  • Logs that appeared to contain autofill information and cryptocurrency wallet data.

Fowler also identified approximately 400,000 documents that appeared to come from malware capable of creating more detailed collections about individual victims.

That makes this more than a list of passwords. Some of the material could help an attacker connect a person’s accounts, identify their device, and potentially access an account where the person was already signed in.

Fowler could not identify the database’s owner. He notified its hosting provider, and public access was restricted several days later. How long it had been exposed, and whether anyone else accessed it, remain unknown.

In the separate discovery, researcher Greg Pollock identified an Elasticsearch server exposing approximately 259 GB of data on people in mainland China. Anyone who knew its address could search it without a password. Its 99 indices contained almost 1.64 billion records linking names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, student information, and business registrations. These included at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers and about 11 million student enrollment records. Some student records linked a child’s name to their school, class, and a parent’s contact details.

This database brought together information from identity registration, education, telecommunications, payment, and business systems. Based on how the records were organized, UpGuard believes someone combined them to create an illicit identity-lookup service.

Pollock could not identify the operator. During his investigation, the server became inaccessible, apparently following a ransomware or other destructive attack. Other copies of the data may still exist.

Are your details being used by cybercriminals? 

FIND OUT HERE

How to stay safe

If malware stole your login details, changing affected passwords is a good start. Use a clean device to make those changes, and sign out of existing sessions in case someone also has the cookies that keep you logged in.

  • Check for infection. Run a scan with a trusted anti-malware product. If you suspect an active infostealer infection, disconnect the affected device and use a separate, clean device for urgent account recovery. Otherwise, malware could capture replacement passwords too.
  • Secure your most important accounts first. Start with your primary email, followed by banking, payment, work, and other sensitive accounts. Replace exposed or reused passwords with unique ones, using a password manager to generate and store them.
  • Enable multifactor authentication. An authenticator app or security key adds protection against someone signing in with a stolen password.
  • Sign out existing sessions. Look in your account’s security settings for an option such as “sign out everywhere,” “log out of all devices,” or “revoke active sessions.” Removing malware and changing passwords do not necessarily stop someone using an already stolen session token.
  • Watch for financial and identity misuse. Review account activity and credit reports for transactions or accounts you don’t recognize.
  • Review unsolicited messages with extra care. If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard. It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next.

You can replace a password. Details like the school you attended can stay useful to scammers for years. If an unexpected caller or message mentions something personal, verify who you’re dealing with before sharing information or sending money.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. 
 
Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

items.title: Agents you didn’t deploy can still read your data
items.summary: On October 15, India’s national CERT, CERT-In, issued a critical advisory. Two weeks later, on October 30, Chainalysis disclosed that it had detected an external actor using “offensive agentic techniques” to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools. It found no indication that investigation content, clear-text passwords, MFA secrets, or session tokens were accessed. Some customer account details, such as user IDs, names, and email addresses, were accessed. Source: Chainalysis, Security Incident Information , Oct. 2026. Neither case involved an agent the victim deployed. Controls built around your own agents don’t reach agents someone else is running. Cyera Endpoint extends the controls to devices. Securiti, Feb. 2026 Agent Commander, introduced with Veeam, detects AI risk, applies runtime guardrails, and can roll back what an agent did. Immuta, Mar. 2026 Agentic Data Access gives agents their own identity, attributes, intent, and audit trail, and grants access when it is needed instead of as standing privilege. OneTrust, Sept. 2026 CORIE enforces enterprise policy at runtime while agents work, and records their decisions. Informatica, May 2026 Agent Fabric Context Catalog: one place to discover, govern, and operate data assets and AI agents together. Read the verbs Inventory. Detect. Monitor. Govern. Enforce. The other side of the argument Most of the field is fencing the agent. We fence the data. CERT-In says these agents got in using credentials left in application configuration and public code repositories, and cloud roles with too much access. A credential like that opens what that identity can open. It doesn’t come with a key unless that identity was given one. Protection on the data changes what they find. When PK Protect encrypts a supported file, the protection stays on the file after it moves. PK Protect’s key management issues the keys, and your directory groups decide who can use them. We enforce policy at runtime. What happens to the file when the policy is not in the path, or fails? Agents get least-privilege access. Is the file still protected after an authorized agent copies it somewhere? One control plane for people, machines, and agents. Can the same platform encrypt, mask, or redact the data, or does it report on it? Request your assessment
