items.title: How did pinwheel calculators work?
items.summary: As a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd . I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace. A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of these designs, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection: In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register (top), turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d instead turn the crank counterclockwise. The second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value. To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator. Alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism: Calculator entrails. By author. There’s a lot going on here, but the most important part of the assembly is the cylindrical stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detent positions: The fundamental mechanism of a pinwheel calculator. By author. Each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever one way or the other, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly. Input digit set to “3”, with three pins extended. By author. When the crank is turned, the entire assembly rotates and these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator: Of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear — offset to the right — so it has no effect on the output value. To actually perform carry, each digit of the accumulator is equipped with a cam that shoves a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the value rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge in turn deflects the carry pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit. This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video: The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the home position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus resetting the mechanism. Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1). There’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this ancient YouTube video provides a more complete walkthrough. And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article: PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs, used as the implicit destination for some opcodes, is called the “accumulator”. items.title: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall
items.summary: AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules , which match traffic by the AWS resources that send and receive it instead of by IP address. A rule can name a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, a security group, or a transit gateway attachment. Rules that match on IP addresses have to keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with. A VPC-attached AWS Lambda function can scale out and start sending traffic before an updated IP list reaches the firewall. With context-aware rules, you can filter a function’s traffic by the security group attached to it. With context-aware rules, you can: Write rules that follow your workloads – A rule that names a security group applies to each new resource whose network interface has that security group attached. A rule that names a subnet or VPC applies to each new resource that you launch in it. A rule that names a transit gateway attachment applies to traffic that enters through that attachment. Apply one policy across accounts – One context store tracks the resources in the accounts that attach to a shared transit gateway. A rule can name context from any of those accounts. See which resources are behind each connection – Your firewall logs record the resources on each side of a flow, along with their IP addresses. In this post, we explain how context-aware rules work, set them up across accounts, and show what the logs record. How context-aware rules work Context-aware rules require transit gateway-attached firewalls , and they combine a control path and a data path (Figure 1). On the control path, a context store tells the firewall which AWS resources exist. On the data path, the transit gateway adds the context of the sender to each packet. The firewall brings the two together and matches that context against your rules. Figure 1: How context-aware rules work across accounts A context store tracks your resources. A context store is a catalog of the AWS resources that can send and receive traffic through a transit gateway. You create it in AWS Network Manager and associate it with the transit gateway that your firewall uses. When you share the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) , those accounts create transit gateway VPC attachments to it. The context of those attachments, and of the resources behind them, then appears in the same context store. The context store is designed to keep the firewall in sync as you add and remove resources. The transit gateway tags each packet. When traffic crosses the transit gateway, the transit gateway tags each packet with the context of the resource that sent it. That context is the sender’s VPC, subnet, transit gateway attachment, and the security groups attached to the sender. The firewall gets only the security group IDs, not their rules, so a rule that names any one of those groups matches. The firewall matches context IDs in your rules. It reads the context on each packet and matches it against your rules. You group context IDs into a context set , a named rule variable that lists resources from the context store associated with the firewall. Then you use the set in the source or destination of a rule, in a Classic or Next Generation firewall policy . Source context works with every protocol, because each packet carries the context of its sender. Destination context requires TCP-based rules, because the firewall learns the receiving resource from return traffic. For more details, see How context-aware rules work and Matching on destination context . AWS Transit Gateway also shares context with third-party firewalls through Gateway Load Balancer . For that setup, see Introducing resource context for firewall policies with AWS Transit Gateway . Getting started In this example, a central networking account owns the transit gateway and the firewall, and shares the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS RAM. You complete steps 1 and 2 once, in the account that owns the transit gateway. 1. Create a context store. In the AWS Network Manager console , select or create a global network and register your transit gateway with it. Then create a context store and associate it with the transit gateway (). Network Firewall discovers the context store on its own, so there’s nothing to configure on the firewall. Figure 2: A context store associated with a transit gateway 2. Give Network Firewall access to the context store. In the account that owns the context store, create the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role NetworkFirewallContextStoreReadOnly . Use the trust policy and permissions in Onboarding your transit gateway to a context store . You create the role once for each account that owns a context store. 3. Create a context set. In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console , under Network Firewall , create a rule group. On the Rule group variables page, choose Create context set , select your context store, and select the resources for the set. One set can mix context IDs of different resource types, from the accounts in the context store. Figure 3: Creating a context set from the resources that the context store tracks 4. Check the sync state. Before you write rules, open the firewall’s details page and check the Context store sync state section. It shows the context store that the firewall discovered and its sync state. Figure 4: The context store sync state on the firewall’s details page 5. Use the context set in your rules. The sample rule from Writing context-aware rules blocks SSH from PROD_RESOURCES to destinations outside your home networks. In a Next Generation firewall rule group, on the Configure rules page, use the Visual rule builder . Choose Drop and TCP . For Sources , choose Match specific criteria , select Context sets , and choose PROD_RESOURCES . For Destinations, choose Match specific criteria , select Destination IP , and enter $EXTERNAL_NET . Set the destination port to 22. Then add the rule group to your firewall policy. Figure 5: Choosing a context set as a rule’s source in the Next Generation rule builder The same rule in Suricata-compatible syntax follows. drop:flow is the action and its scope, tcp:all the protocol and connection state, and the rest is the source, destination, and port. In raw rules, you reference a context set with $ and its name; in the console, you pick it from a list. drop:flow tcp:all $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001;) Because the rule names resources and not addresses, it covers each new resource that you launch in those VPCs or attach that security group to. For Classic policies, the same rule looks like this: drop tcp $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001; rev:1;) What the logs record After you associate the transit gateway with a context store, Network Firewall adds a context object to its alert log and flow log records. The following records, shortened, show one outbound TLS connection from an application instance to example.com, through a central egress VPC with a network address translation (NAT) gateway. A rule that references the application’s security group blocks the connection and writes this alert log record. The matched list names the security group that the rule matched. { "event": { "event_type": "alert", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "context": { "matched": [ "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ] }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2002, "signature": "Application A: domain not on its allow list" } } } The flow log record for the same flow_id lists the full context on each side. The src list holds the sender’s context IDs. Flow logs record this context for every flow, even when no rule matches it. { "event": { "event_type": "netflow", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "context": { "src": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60011", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60021", "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ], "dst": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60003", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60013", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60023" ] } } } The dst list shows how destination context works for traffic to the internet. The firewall learns the destination from the response, and the response reaches the firewall from the NAT gateway. So the destination context is the egress VPC, the NAT gateway’s subnet, and the egress VPC’s transit gateway attachment, not the internet host. You can query these fields by context ID in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights . For example, you can see what an application already connects to before you write its rules. For the fields, see Context in your network firewall logs . Availability and pricing Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge. Standard AWS Network Firewall and AWS Transit Gateway charges apply to the resources that you use. For details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing and AWS Transit Gateway pricing . They work in the AWS Regions where both Network Firewall and Transit Gateway context sharing are available. Conclusion In this post, we showed how you can use context-aware rules in Network Firewall to match traffic on the context of the resources that send and receive traffic. A context store tracks those resources across the accounts that share your transit gateway, and the transit gateway tags each packet with its sender’s context. Your rules and logs then use that context, so your rules can keep up as workloads change. To learn more, see Context-aware rules in AWS Network Firewall . If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Lawton Pittenger Lawton is a Worldwide Security Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York City. He helps customers design and implement effective network security controls, and works with AWS service teams to improve security services based on customer feedback. Outside of work, he enjoys skateboarding, snowboarding, and spending time in nature. Santosh Shanbhag Santosh is a seasoned product leader, specializing in security, data protection, and compliance. At AWS, he focuses on securing workloads through Network and Application Security services, including AWS Network Firewall and active threat defense. Rahi Patel Rahi is a Startups Technical Account Manager at AWS specializing in Networking. He architects cloud networking solutions, optimizing performance across global AWS deployments. Previously a network engineer with Cisco Meraki, he holds an MS in Engineering from San Jose State University. Outside work, he enjoys tennis and pickleball. Mahesh Elireddy Mahesh is a Senior Software Development Engineer at AWS, where he has spent 10 years building the network. He has been a part of the teams that built Network Load Balancer, Gateway Load Balancer, and NAT Gateway, and now works on AWS Network Firewall. Outside of work, he likes spending time outdoors in the Pacific Northwest with his family.

Then create a context store and associate it with the transit gateway (). Network Firewall discovers the context store on its own, so there’s nothing to configure on the firewall.

Figure 2: A context store associated with a transit gateway

2. Give Network Firewall access to the context store. In the account that owns the context store, create the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role NetworkFirewallContextStoreReadOnly. Use the trust policy and permissions in Onboarding your transit gateway to a context store. You create the role once for each account that owns a context store.

3. Create a context set. In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, create a rule group. On the Rule group variables page, choose Create context set, select your context store, and select the resources for the set. One set can mix context IDs of different resource types, from the accounts in the context store.

Figure 3: Creating a context set from the resources that the context store tracks

4. Check the sync state. Before you write rules, open the firewall’s details page and check the Context store sync state section. It shows the context store that the firewall discovered and its sync state.

Figure 4: The context store sync state on the firewall’s details page

5. Use the context set in your rules. The sample rule from Writing context-aware rules blocks SSH from PROD_RESOURCES to destinations outside your home networks. In a Next Generation firewall rule group, on the Configure rules page, use the Visual rule builder. Choose Drop and TCP. For Sources, choose Match specific criteria, select Context sets, and choose PROD_RESOURCES. For Destinations, choose Match specific criteria, select Destination IP, and enter $EXTERNAL_NET. Set the destination port to 22. Then add the rule group to your firewall policy.

Figure 5: Choosing a context set as a rule’s source in the Next Generation rule builder

The same rule in Suricata-compatible syntax follows. drop:flow is the action and its scope, tcp:all the protocol and connection state, and the rest is the source, destination, and port. In raw rules, you reference a context set with $ and its name; in the console, you pick it from a list.

drop:flow tcp:all $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001;)

Because the rule names resources and not addresses, it covers each new resource that you launch in those VPCs or attach that security group to.

For Classic policies, the same rule looks like this:

drop tcp $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001; rev:1;)
What the logs record

After you associate the transit gateway with a context store, Network Firewall adds a context object to its alert log and flow log records. The following records, shortened, show one outbound TLS connection from an application instance to example.com, through a central egress VPC with a network address translation (NAT) gateway. A rule that references the application’s security group blocks the connection and writes this alert log record. The matched list names the security group that the rule matched.

{
  "event": {
    "event_type": "alert",
    "flow_id": 314246768212473,
    "src_ip": "10.1.1.25",
    "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "app_proto": "tls",
    "tls": {
      "sni": "example.com"
    },
    "context": {
      "matched": [
        "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031"
      ]
    },
    "alert": {
      "action": "blocked",
      "signature_id": 2002,
      "signature": "Application A: domain not on its allow list"
    }
  }
}

The flow log record for the same flow_id lists the full context on each side. The src list holds the sender’s context IDs. Flow logs record this context for every flow, even when no rule matches it.

{
  "event": {
    "event_type": "netflow",
    "flow_id": 314246768212473,
    "src_ip": "10.1.1.25",
    "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "app_proto": "tls",
    "context": {
      "src": [
        "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001",
        "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60011",
        "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60021",
        "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031"
      ],
      "dst": [
        "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60003",
        "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60013",
        "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60023"
      ]
    }
  }
}

The dst list shows how destination context works for traffic to the internet. The firewall learns the destination from the response, and the response reaches the firewall from the NAT gateway. So the destination context is the egress VPC, the NAT gateway’s subnet, and the egress VPC’s transit gateway attachment, not the internet host. You can query these fields by context ID in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For example, you can see what an application already connects to before you write its rules. For the fields, see Context in your network firewall logs.

Availability and pricing

Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge. Standard AWS Network Firewall and AWS Transit Gateway charges apply to the resources that you use. For details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing and AWS Transit Gateway pricing. They work in the AWS Regions where both Network Firewall and Transit Gateway context sharing are available.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how you can use context-aware rules in Network Firewall to match traffic on the context of the resources that send and receive traffic. A context store tracks those resources across the accounts that share your transit gateway, and the transit gateway tags each packet with its sender’s context. Your rules and logs then use that context, so your rules can keep up as workloads change. To learn more, see Context-aware rules in AWS Network Firewall.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.title: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy
items.summary: When it comes to inspecting network traffic, many security teams want two things from a firewall. They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats. Today, you can do both with AWS Network Firewall , a stateful, managed network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service. In a Classic policy , your access rules and your threat rules run together in one stateful engine and share one rule capacity. With Next Generation policies , access control and threat protection each get their own engine in the same firewall. A firewall engine allows the traffic you approve and drops the rest. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) engine checks the allowed traffic with AWS managed rule groups or with rules that you write. Each engine has its own rule capacity , so adding access rules doesn’t take capacity away from threat protection. In this post, we walk through what Next Generation policies are, how they evaluate traffic, and the new concepts they introduce. We use sample records to cover what each engine logs and how to validate a policy with the new monitor mode. To put it all together, we walk through creating an example Next Generation policy. How a Next Generation policy works A Next Generation policy inspects traffic with two engines , in sequence. Traffic that the firewall engine allows moves to the IPS engine, and traffic that the firewall engine blocks goes no further. The firewall engine is drop by default, and the IPS engine is pass by default. If you already write Suricata rules, the two engines will feel familiar. The firewall engine is built on Suricata 8 firewall mode , which follows each connection as it progresses and evaluates rules at each step. The IPS engine uses the Suricata compatible intrusion detection system (IDS) and IPS rules that you already know from the stateful engine in a Classic policy, with one difference: it evaluates rules in action order and doesn’t support Classic options such as strict order. A Classic policy uses a stateless engine and then a stateful engine that evaluates access rules and threat rules together. In a Next Generation policy, both engines are stateful, so each rule is evaluated with full connection context, which helps keep traffic handling consistent and predictable. The firewall engine works up to the application layer. It follows each connection for its entire flow, from the first packet through the TCP handshake and application layer exchanges such as the TLS client hello, and evaluates your access rules along the way (Figure 1). Figure 1: Classic and Next Generation policy engines and their rule capacity. This separation changes how you design a policy. Because each engine has one job, you can plan access control and threat protection on their own, and different teams can work independently. For example, a networking team can manage access rules while a security team handles threat detection, and neither has to rewrite the other’s rules. The firewall engine controls access You configure access control by specifying an action for a protocol, along with a source and destination. Rules run in the order that you set . Traffic that no rule allows gets the policy’s firewall default action , which is drop unless you change it. In a Next Generation policy, the drop default action applies from the first packet, so for TCP traffic the firewall can drop the initial SYN. Unlike the drop established default action in a Classic policy, it doesn’t wait for a connection to be established. A few terms explain how the firewall engine evaluates traffic. Connection states are the protocol states that a connection progresses through, such as the TCP handshake and the TLS client hello. A hook is the point at a connection state where your rules attach, so a rule’s hook sets when the firewall engine evaluates it. Each rule also has an action , such as accept, drop, or reject. Its action scope sets how much of the traffic the action applies to, from one packet or one transaction up to the whole connection, called the flow . For more details, see Firewall engine hooks . When you build a rule in the console, you choose a protocol and then two settings: Connection state , which sets the rule’s hook, and Action scope . For example, to allow a domain over TLS, you match its server name at the Client Hello connection state with the This flow action scope. Because the firewall engine is drop by default, a connection advances to the next connection state only while your rules keep accepting it. For example, a connection can pass the TCP handshake and still be dropped at the TLS client hello. That happens when its server name isn’t on your approved list (Figure 2). Figure 2: A connection is accepted at the TCP handshake hook and dropped at the TLS client hello hook. In Figure 2, the rule for www.amazon.com accepts the flow when it matches the server name at the TLS client hello hook. No rule accepts example.com at that hook, so the firewall default action drops it. You don’t have to write every rule in raw Suricata syntax. You can build rules in the console rule builder, or, as in the example later in this post, enter your domains in a domain list rule group, and Network Firewall builds the rules for you. Action scope also sets where an accepted connection goes next. An accept with the hook scope allows the connection to advance to the next connection state, where the rules at that hook evaluate it. An accept with the flow scope lets the connection skip the remaining hooks and move to the IPS engine (Figure 3). A firewall rule can also bypass the IPS engine for specific traffic when you choose. For the valid combinations of action and scope at each type of hook, see Firewall engine actions and scopes . Figure 3: An accept with the hook scope compared with an accept with the flow scope. The IPS engine looks for threats Traffic that the firewall engine allows then reaches the IPS engine , which inspects it with Suricata compatible rules. The IPS engine is designed to look for specific threats, so it blocks only traffic that matches a threat rule. IPS rules evaluate in action order . Pass rules go first, then drop, reject, and alert rules, regardless of the order in which you define them. For the full path through both engines, see How Network Firewall filters traffic with a Next Generation policy . We recommend that you start with the AWS managed rule groups . Because the IPS engine is built on the industry standard Suricata engine, you can also run Suricata compatible rule sets from specialized security providers, alongside rules that you write yourself. Referenced rule groups and embedded rules Each engine gets its rules from its own section of the policy . You can add rules in two ways and mix both in one section. Referenced rule groups are separate resources, and they’re the only kind of rule group that Classic policies support. You create a rule group once and add it to as many policies as you need. You can also share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) . For details, see Sharing AWS Network Firewall resources . When you update the rule group, each policy that references it picks up the change. You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow. Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas . Read what each engine logs Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration . Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened. The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list. { "firewall_name": "example-fw", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event_timestamp": "1794341434", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "app_proto": "tls", "src_ip": "10.0.1.25", "src_port": 42698, "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "alert": { "engine": "fw", "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2201001, "signature": "SURICATA FW default app policy", "severity": 3 }, "firewall": { "hook": "tls:client_hello", "policy": "drop:flow,alert" }, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "aws_metadata": { "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy" }, "timestamp": "2026-11-10T20:10:34.141643+0000" } } The following table explains the key fields in this record. Field Value What it tells you alert.engine fw The firewall engine wrote this record. firewall.hook tls:client_hello The decision happened at the TLS client hello, where the client sends the server name example.com. alert.signature SURICATA FW default app policy No rule matched, so the firewall default action applied. The default action logs its drops on its own, so you don’t need an alert rule to see what it blocks. firewall.policy drop:flow,alert The action and scope that applied. The default action dropped the whole flow and wrote an alert. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The policy itself is the source, because the record doesn’t come from one of your rule groups. When a connection that the firewall engine allowed matches a threat rule, the IPS engine writes its own record. In this test, the firewall engine allowed TLS to one test server by IP address. The IPS section also held the following embedded rule, which drops TLS connections with a JA4 fingerprint that your threat intelligence flags. The fingerprint in this rule is a sample value: drop tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"; flow:to_server,established; ja4.hash; content:"t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:900002; rev:1;) This is a sample rule to show the IPS engine at work. In your own policies, we recommend that you start with the AWS managed threat signature rule groups and add custom rules where you need them. A test client with that fingerprint connected to that server without a server name, and the IPS engine wrote the following record. { "firewall_name": "example-fw", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event_timestamp": "1794377726", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "app_proto": "tls", "src_ip": "10.0.1.25", "src_port": 38342, "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "tls": { "version": "TLS 1.3", "ja4": "t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb" }, "alert": { "engine": "td", "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 900002, "signature": "Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"", "category": "A Network Trojan was detected", "severity": 1 }, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "aws_metadata": { "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy" }, "timestamp": "2026-11-11T06:15:26.671435+0000" } } Field Value What it tells you alert.engine td The IPS engine wrote this record. IPS records have no firewall object, because IPS rules don’t use hooks. tls.ja4 t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb The JA4 fingerprint of the client, which matches the fingerprint in the rule. alert.signature Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4) The IPS rule that matched, from the rule’s msg option. alert.category A Network Trojan was detected The rule’s classtype, trojan-activity, sets this category. verdict.action drop The IPS engine dropped the connection. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The rule is embedded in the policy, so the record shows the policy ARN. A match from an AWS managed rule group or one of your referenced rule groups carries that rule group’s ARN instead. To separate access control events from threat events in your queries, filter on the engine field. To find which rule group produced an event, use resource_arn. Embedded rules and the default action show the policy ARN. Validate in monitor mode, then enforce Each Next Generation policy has a policy mode , enforce or monitor. In enforce mode, the engines apply their actions. In monitor mode, both engines evaluate your traffic and log what they would do. Your rules and the default action don’t drop or reject traffic. Monitor mode also turns on alert logging for your rules and the default action, so each firewall rule that would block traffic logs its matches. That makes monitor mode a lower-risk way to stage a rollout of a new policy or a change to an existing one. Monitor logs are close to enforce mode but can differ. When a firewall rule would block a connection, monitor mode lets the connection through but sends it past the IPS engine, just as a blocked connection never reaches the IPS engine in enforce mode. So the monitor logs don’t show IPS alerts for that connection. For the full list of differences, see Policy mode: enforce and monitor . To validate a policy in monitor mode: Set Policy mode to Monitor , and confirm that alert logging is on for the firewall. Amazon Route 53 Resolved IP Validation still applies its configured action in monitor mode, so if your policy uses it, set its action to Alert . Send representative traffic for long enough to cover your normal patterns. In your alert logs, filter on engine = fw. Check the FirewallDefaultActionApplied metric in Amazon CloudWatch . Traffic that you meant to allow shouldn’t be reaching the default action. When the results look right, switch Policy mode to Enforce during a maintenance window. Changing the policy mode or the firewall default action restarts stateful inspection on the firewall, which interrupts established connections. Example policy with a domain allow list and threat protection The following example puts the engines, logs, and monitor mode together. It allows outbound traffic only to approved domains and checks that allowed traffic for known threats. The firewall engine holds the domain allow list, and the IPS engine runs the AWS active threat defense managed rule group . Figure 4 shows the policy and where each of the earlier log records comes from. Log record 2 comes from the sample embedded rule, which isn’t part of the policy that you create in the following steps. Figure 4: The example policy, with the sample embedded rule behind log record 2. To create the domain list rule group: In the Network Firewall console, choose Network Firewall rule groups , and then choose Create rule group . Choose Next Generation as the rule group version, Firewall rule group as the type, and Domain list as the format. Figure 5: Choosing the rule group version, type, and format for the domain list. Enter one domain per line, for example .amazon.com and checkip.amazonaws.com , and under Protocols , select HTTPS only. For HTTPS, the firewall matches the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) without decrypting traffic. SNI is the server name that a client sends at the start of a TLS connection. To include a domain and its subdomains, start the name with a dot. For Capacity sizing , choose Allow room to grow , and then create the rule group. To create the policy: Choose Firewall policies , and then choose Create firewall policy . Select Next Generation as the policy version and Drop as the firewall default action, so the firewall blocks traffic that you don’t allow. Set Policy mode to Monitor . We recommend rolling out a new policy in monitor mode first, then switching to enforce after you validate it. Enable Active Threat Defense is selected by default. Active threat defense is optional. Additional charges apply; for details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing . Figure 6: The policy details page, with Next Generation, Drop, and Monitor selected. On the Add firewall rule groups step, add the domain list rule group that you created in the previous procedure. On the Add IPS rule groups step, the active threat defense managed rule group, listed as AttackInfrastructure , is already added. It comes from the Enable Active Threat Defense default that Figure 6 shows. Choose Add rule group to add more AWS managed rule groups , your own rule groups, or embedded rules. Create the policy, associate it with your firewall, and turn on alert and flow logging . After you validate the policy, as described in Validate in monitor mode, then enforce, switch Policy mode to Enforce . For more detail, see Creating a rule group for a Next Generation policy and Generating firewall rules from domain names . Already using Classic policies? Classic Network Firewall policies remain supported, and your existing firewalls keep running as they are. Each firewall uses one policy type at a time, either a Classic policy or a Next Generation policy. For new firewalls, we recommend Next Generation policies. We’re working on migration guidance for existing policies, so you can plan a move when it suits you. To try one now, create a test firewall with a Next Generation policy and start it in monitor mode. To compare the two policy types, see AWS Network Firewall firewall policy versions . Next Generation policies are available at no additional charge. You pay the standard Network Firewall charges for your firewall endpoints and the traffic they process. For Regions and pricing, see AWS Services by Region and AWS Network Firewall pricing . Conclusion In this post, we showed you how a Next Generation policy gives access control and threat protection separate engines, each with its own rule capacity, so you can grow your firewall rules and IPS rules independently. We also showed what each engine logs, how to validate a policy in monitor mode, and how to build a policy that allows only approved domains and checks the allowed traffic for threats. To learn more, see Getting started with a Next Generation policy , and to automate your policies, use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDKs . If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . He helps customers design and implement effective network security controls, and works with AWS service teams to improve security services based on customer feedback. Outside of work, he enjoys skateboarding, snowboarding, and spending time in nature. Santosh Shanbhag Santosh is a seasoned product leader, specializing in security, data protection, and compliance. At AWS, he focuses on securing workloads through Network and Application Security services, including AWS Network Firewall and active threat defense. Aneesh Patel Aneesh is a Software Development Engineer at AWS, based in Herndon, Virginia. He builds and maintains AWS Network Firewall, a managed service that helps customers protect their VPC networks. Outside of work, he enjoys snowboarding, working out, and playing video games.

You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow.

Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas.

Read what each engine logs

Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration. Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened.

The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list.

{
  "firewall_name": "example-fw",
  "availability_zone": "us-east-1a",
  "event_timestamp": "1794341434",
  "event": {
    "event_type": "alert",
    "app_proto": "tls",
    "src_ip": "10.0.1.25",
    "src_port": 42698,
    "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "proto": "TCP",
    "tls": {
      "sni": "example.com"
    },
    "alert": {
      "engine": "fw",
      "action": "blocked",
      "signature_id": 2201001,
      "signature": "SURICATA FW default app policy",
      "severity": 3
    },
    "firewall": {
      "hook": "tls:client_hello",
      "policy": "drop:flow,alert"
    },
    "verdict": {
      "action": "drop"
    },
    "aws_metadata": {
      "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy"
    },
    "timestamp": "2026-11-10T20:10:34.141643+0000"
  }
}

The following table explains the key fields in this record.

Field Value What it tells you alert.engine fw The firewall engine wrote this record. firewall.hook tls:client_hello The decision happened at the TLS client hello, where the client sends the server name example.com. alert.signature SURICATA FW default app policy No rule matched, so the firewall default action applied. The default action logs its drops on its own, so you don’t need an alert rule to see what it blocks. firewall.policy drop:flow,alert The action and scope that applied. The default action dropped the whole flow and wrote an alert. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The policy itself is the source, because the record doesn’t come from one of your rule groups.

When a connection that the firewall engine allowed matches a threat rule, the IPS engine writes its own record. In this test, the firewall engine allowed TLS to one test server by IP address. The IPS section also held the following embedded rule, which drops TLS connections with a JA4 fingerprint that your threat intelligence flags. The fingerprint in this rule is a sample value:

drop tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"; flow:to_server,established; ja4.hash; content:"t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:900002; rev:1;)

This is a sample rule to show the IPS engine at work. In your own policies, we recommend that you start with the AWS managed threat signature rule groups and add custom rules where you need them.

A test client with that fingerprint connected to that server without a server name, and the IPS engine wrote the following record.

{
  "firewall_name": "example-fw",
  "availability_zone": "us-east-1a",
  "event_timestamp": "1794377726",
  "event": {
    "event_type": "alert",
    "app_proto": "tls",
    "src_ip": "10.0.1.25",
    "src_port": 38342,
    "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7",
    "dest_port": 443,
    "proto": "TCP",
    "tls": {
      "version": "TLS 1.3",
      "ja4": "t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"
    },
    "alert": {
      "engine": "td",
      "action": "blocked",
      "signature_id": 900002,
      "signature": "Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"",
      "category": "A Network Trojan was detected",
      "severity": 1
    },
    "verdict": {
      "action": "drop"
    },
    "aws_metadata": {
      "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy"
    },
    "timestamp": "2026-11-11T06:15:26.671435+0000"
  }
}
Field Value What it tells you alert.engine td The IPS engine wrote this record. IPS records have no firewall object, because IPS rules don’t use hooks. tls.ja4 t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb The JA4 fingerprint of the client, which matches the fingerprint in the rule. alert.signature Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4) The IPS rule that matched, from the rule’s msg option. alert.category A Network Trojan was detected The rule’s classtype, trojan-activity, sets this category. verdict.action drop The IPS engine dropped the connection. aws_metadata.resource_arn arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy The rule is embedded in the policy, so the record shows the policy ARN. A match from an AWS managed rule group or one of your referenced rule groups carries that rule group’s ARN instead.

To separate access control events from threat events in your queries, filter on the engine field. To find which rule group produced an event, use resource_arn. Embedded rules and the default action show the policy ARN.

Validate in monitor mode, then enforce

Each Next Generation policy has a policy mode, enforce or monitor. In enforce mode, the engines apply their actions. In monitor mode, both engines evaluate your traffic and log what they would do. Your rules and the default action don’t drop or reject traffic.

Monitor mode also turns on alert logging for your rules and the default action, so each firewall rule that would block traffic logs its matches. That makes monitor mode a lower-risk way to stage a rollout of a new policy or a change to an existing one. Monitor logs are close to enforce mode but can differ. When a firewall rule would block a connection, monitor mode lets the connection through but sends it past the IPS engine, just as a blocked connection never reaches the IPS engine in enforce mode. So the monitor logs don’t show IPS alerts for that connection. For the full list of differences, see Policy mode: enforce and monitor.

To validate a policy in monitor mode:

  1. Set Policy mode to Monitor, and confirm that alert logging is on for the firewall. Amazon Route 53 Resolved IP Validation still applies its configured action in monitor mode, so if your policy uses it, set its action to Alert.
  2. Send representative traffic for long enough to cover your normal patterns.
  3. In your alert logs, filter on engine = fw. Check the FirewallDefaultActionApplied metric in Amazon CloudWatch. Traffic that you meant to allow shouldn’t be reaching the default action.
  4. When the results look right, switch Policy mode to Enforce during a maintenance window. Changing the policy mode or the firewall default action restarts stateful inspection on the firewall, which interrupts established connections.
Example policy with a domain allow list and threat protection

The following example puts the engines, logs, and monitor mode together. It allows outbound traffic only to approved domains and checks that allowed traffic for known threats. The firewall engine holds the domain allow list, and the IPS engine runs the AWS active threat defense managed rule group. Figure 4 shows the policy and where each of the earlier log records comes from. Log record 2 comes from the sample embedded rule, which isn’t part of the policy that you create in the following steps.

Figure 4: The example policy, with the sample embedded rule behind log record 2.

To create the domain list rule group:

  1. In the Network Firewall console, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Next Generation as the rule group version, Firewall rule group as the type, and Domain list as the format.

    Figure 5: Choosing the rule group version, type, and format for the domain list.

  2. Enter one domain per line, for example .amazon.com and checkip.amazonaws.com, and under Protocols, select HTTPS only. For HTTPS, the firewall matches the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) without decrypting traffic. SNI is the server name that a client sends at the start of a TLS connection. To include a domain and its subdomains, start the name with a dot.
  3. For Capacity sizing, choose Allow room to grow, and then create the rule group.

To create the policy:

  1. Choose Firewall policies, and then choose Create firewall policy. Select Next Generation as the policy version and Drop as the firewall default action, so the firewall blocks traffic that you don’t allow. Set Policy mode to Monitor. We recommend rolling out a new policy in monitor mode first, then switching to enforce after you validate it. Enable Active Threat Defense is selected by default. Active threat defense is optional. Additional charges apply; for details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing.

    Figure 6: The policy details page, with Next Generation, Drop, and Monitor selected.

  2. On the Add firewall rule groups step, add the domain list rule group that you created in the previous procedure.
  3. On the Add IPS rule groups step, the active threat defense managed rule group, listed as AttackInfrastructure, is already added. It comes from the Enable Active Threat Defense default that Figure 6 shows. Choose Add rule group to add more AWS managed rule groups, your own rule groups, or embedded rules.
  4. Create the policy, associate it with your firewall, and turn on alert and flow logging.
  5. After you validate the policy, as described in Validate in monitor mode, then enforce, switch Policy mode to Enforce.

For more detail, see Creating a rule group for a Next Generation policy and Generating firewall rules from domain names.

Already using Classic policies?

Classic Network Firewall policies remain supported, and your existing firewalls keep running as they are. Each firewall uses one policy type at a time, either a Classic policy or a Next Generation policy. For new firewalls, we recommend Next Generation policies. We’re working on migration guidance for existing policies, so you can plan a move when it suits you.

To try one now, create a test firewall with a Next Generation policy and start it in monitor mode. To compare the two policy types, see AWS Network Firewall firewall policy versions. Next Generation policies are available at no additional charge. You pay the standard Network Firewall charges for your firewall endpoints and the traffic they process. For Regions and pricing, see AWS Services by Region and AWS Network Firewall pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how a Next Generation policy gives access control and threat protection separate engines, each with its own rule capacity, so you can grow your firewall rules and IPS rules independently. We also showed what each engine logs, how to validate a policy in monitor mode, and how to build a policy that allows only approved domains and checks the allowed traffic for threats. To learn more, see Getting started with a Next Generation policy, and to automate your policies, use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDKs.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.title: Analyzing a SOCKS connection close bug in chisel and revsocks
items.summary: Analyzing a SOCKS connection close bug in chisel and revsocks 25/11/2026 Qualification Chisel and revsocks are among the tools we regularly use at Synacktiv. This is what motivated us to build an automated test suite to verify the reliability of these tools. In this post, we will show how a bug in the implementation of the SOCKS protocol was discovered in a library used by two different projects, and how it was fixed. Learn more

items.title: Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
items.summary: The short version An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password. Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys. We implemented containment measures, restored clean versions of the affected service, and have triggered a rotation of internal credentials. You do not need to update anything in your 1Password account. We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password, such as invitations or account recovery requests that you did not initiate. 1Password apps and services are working normally. What happened On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker. What information was affected The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include: Names and email addresses Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security) Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account) Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers) The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security. When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible. What was not affected Your vaults and the items in them The keys that protect your vaults 1Password does not store your account password or secret key Account recovery keys 1Password apps and browser extensions What we’ve done Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created. Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed. Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure. Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack. Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens. Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts. What you can do Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts. 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. Keep your Secret Key and account password safe. If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com. Our commitment to you You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers. We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.
items.summary_html:
The short version

  • An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password.

  • Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys.

  • We implemented containment measures, restored clean versions of the affected service, and have triggered a rotation of internal credentials.

  • You do not need to update anything in your 1Password account.

  • We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password, such as invitations or account recovery requests that you did not initiate.

  • 1Password apps and services are working normally.

What happened

On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

What information was affected

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

  • Names and email addresses

  • Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

  • Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

  • Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

  • Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

What was not affected

  • Your vaults and the items in them

  • The keys that protect your vaults

    • 1Password does not store your account password or secret key

  • Account recovery keys

  • 1Password apps and browser extensions

What we’ve done

  • Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

  • Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

  • Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

  • Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.

  • Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

  • Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

What you can do

  • Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

  • 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.

  • Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

  • If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

Our commitment to you

You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.
